depth.name: absent
depth.plain: Nothing in the document bears on the behaviour.

depth.name: named
depth.plain: The behaviour is mentioned, usually inside a list or a passage about something else, and nothing further is said about it.

depth.name: discussed
depth.plain: The document takes the behaviour up in its own right and says what it expects and why, in terms too general to grade an answer against.

depth.name: prescribed
depth.plain: The document states concrete do and don't rules, precise enough that anyone testing a model could quote its own sentences as the standard.

depth.name: demonstrated
depth.plain: The rules come with worked cases showing the response the document sanctions, close enough to settle a borderline answer.

depth.name: bounded
depth.plain: Demonstrated, and for every part of the behaviour the document shows where the line falls, names one of its own rules that pulls against this one and says which prevails, and says what to do when the case cannot be decided.

takeaways.title: Six of the ten companies publish no constitution
takeaways.text: As of September 2026, only OpenAI, Alibaba, Anthropic and Microsoft publish a constitution. DeepSeek, Google DeepMind, Meta, Mistral AI, Moonshot AI and xAI publish none, so each of them scores 0.0 out of 10 on every figure of the board. On the final score the four that publish stand at 8.6 out of 10 for OpenAI, 8.1 for Anthropic, 8.0 for Alibaba and 6.3 for Microsoft. The smallest gap between a company that publishes and one that does not is therefore 6.3 points. A zero records what is public. A document of this kind may exist inside a company without having been released, and nobody outside can check a model against it. Publishing leaves two questions open as well. Alibaba's constitution names no model or product that it governs, although it says Alibaba is training its models towards it. Microsoft's is a draft under public consultation, and Microsoft says it is not yet used to train the MAI models it governs.

takeaways.title: Anthropic's constitution goes deepest on the behaviours and trails OpenAI's and Alibaba's as a document
takeaways.text: Anthropic has the highest figure on the behaviours, 8.0 out of 10, ahead of OpenAI on 7.9, Alibaba on 7.5 and Microsoft on 6.1. On the document as a whole it has 8.2 out of 10, against 9.3 for OpenAI, 8.5 for Alibaba and 6.5 for Microsoft, which leaves it second on the final score, 0.1 ahead of Alibaba. Claude's Constitution ranks its four core properties but asks for the order to be weighed as a whole, so it says which should generally prevail and not how a given conflict resolves, and it scores 7.5 out of 10 on clarity when two rules are contradictory, where OpenAI's Model Spec scores 10.0, Alibaba's 8.3 and Microsoft's Code of Conduct also 7.5. Outside its seven hard constraints and its lists of adjustable defaults, a reader often cannot tell a binding rule from a statement of intent, which gives it 6.7 on how firm each rule is, against 9.2 for OpenAI and Alibaba and 7.5 for Microsoft.

takeaways.title: Only Microsoft's Code of Conduct leaves contradictions unsettled
takeaways.text: On unsettled contradictions between rules, OpenAI, Alibaba and Anthropic score 10.0 out of 10 and Microsoft 0.0. Claude's Constitution comes close to one: it asks for professional reticence about the model's own opinions on hot-button issues such as abortion, while the honesty section asks it to share its genuine assessment of hard moral dilemmas and calls a deliberately vague answer given to avoid controversy a breach of honesty. The reticence is stated as a default, and the criterion does not count a default the document allows somebody to change. The referral to emergency services reads like a second contradiction, and is settled by the words that introduce it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct has three, each between two of its guidelines or objectives of the same rank with nothing to say which prevails: an organisation's goals against the rule not to eliminate human roles, a user's topic limits against surfacing the public interest, and the terms a user sets against discouraging emotional dependence. One model found and confirmed them, reading in one session, where each contradiction in the other three documents was found by one of three models and needed two of the three to confirm it.

takeaways.title: Anthropic's constitution explains its rules best and Alibaba's explains them least
takeaways.text: On reasons for the rules, Anthropic scores 9.2 out of 10, OpenAI and Microsoft 7.5 each, and Alibaba 5.8. It is the only criterion of the document as a whole on which Anthropic leads. Nearly every rule in Claude's Constitution that constrains the model says why it exists, in terms specific enough to decide a case the document does not show. OpenAI's reasons run through its chain of command and its agentic, privacy and honesty rules, and are missing from several flat content rules, among them intellectual property, extremism, hate and fairness, as well as from formatting and the preset voice. Microsoft's Code of Conduct argues its rules from one overriding objective, that humans keep meaningful control over AI, and opens each of its Guidelines with its purpose; its bans on weapons, offensive cyberoperations, deepfakes, graphic and romantic content and surveillance give only the reason of their category. Alibaba's rules mostly give their reason in a single clause, and its hard prohibitions give none: the ban on harmful content names the article of the regulation behind it and says no more. Most of its worked examples show where a line falls without saying what the line protects.

takeaways.title: Power and hidden allegiance are the shallowest behaviours in both model specs and in Microsoft's Code of Conduct
takeaways.text: Avoiding illegitimate concentration of power is the lowest behaviour for OpenAI, at 4.0 out of 10, and preventing secret loyalties the lowest for Alibaba, at 2.3; each is the other company's second lowest, at 5.7 and 5.0. OpenAI's Model Spec reaches power through red-line commitments naming persecution, mass surveillance and civic processes, and through one concrete root rule, with worked cases, against political persuasion aimed at particular people or groups. It says nothing on the stakes or reversibility of power, and on loyalty it forbids covert goals in the model's own conduct and says nothing about the models it helps build. Alibaba's gives hidden goals a root rule of its own, and it is one of only three of the document's forty-three rules with no worked example. Claude's Constitution scores 7.0 on power, where it asks how much is at stake and how reversible its concentration would be, and 5.3 on loyalty, where it names the installation of hidden loyalties once and shows no case. Microsoft's Code of Conduct scores 2.0 on power and 2.0 on loyalty, its two lowest. It reaches power through Absolute Constraints on persecution, on unlawful or mass surveillance of civilians and on manipulation at scale, and loyalty through a rule that the model has no goals beyond those of users, operators and the Code and conceals none of its capabilities, even when it infers it is being tested.

takeaways.title: Anthropic's constitution is thinnest on sycophancy and contested questions
takeaways.text: Honesty and non-deception carries the highest figure on the board, 9.3 out of 10 for Anthropic. The two behaviours beside it in its category are where Claude's Constitution is thinnest: 5.3 out of 10 on no sycophancy, level with preventing secret loyalties as its lowest behaviour, and 6.3 on objectivity on contested questions, where OpenAI and Alibaba both score 8.7 and Microsoft 7.0. The two model specs give sycophancy a rule of its own. Microsoft's Code of Conduct gives it one general sentence, softened where an accurate answer might worsen a user's distress, and scores 5.0. Anthropic reaches it through care for wellbeing and through honesty, and does not ask that a factual answer stay the same when the user states a view. On contested questions it makes balance a default an operator may switch off, and shows it on a single case, a persuasive essay whose caveat a user may waive. Anthropic's figure for the honesty and epistemics category is 7.0, its lowest of the four categories.

takeaways.title: No behaviour reaches the top of the depth scale in any constitution
takeaways.text: A depth of 10 asks that, for every part of a behaviour, the document shows where the line falls, names one of its own rules that pulls against it and says which prevails, and says what to do when a case cannot be decided. None of the 56 behaviour figures of the four published constitutions reaches it, and the highest is 9.3, Anthropic on honesty and non-deception. OpenAI, Alibaba and Anthropic agree most closely on instruction-hierarchy conformance, 9.0 out of 10 for OpenAI and 8.7 for Alibaba and Anthropic, and on how to approach tradeoffs, where all three score 8.7; Microsoft scores 7.0 on each. Anthropic reaches that 8.7 with an order of priorities it asks to be weighed as a whole: worked cases settle particular clashes, and there is no general rule for two rules of the same rank. Microsoft's Code of Conduct gives safety and human control strict precedence and leaves a clash between its other Objectives to its Guidelines and to a reading of the Code as a whole.

criteria.name: Clarity when two rules are contradictory
criteria.what_it_is:
Asks whether the document says **in general** which of its own rules prevails when two of them point to different answers, so that a reader can work out the winner in advance.

The full answer is:
- a **strict order of authority** that settles any pair
- a rule for two rules of equal rank
- cases showing the order applied

Unsettled contradictions between rules asks a different question, about the places this machinery does not reach.
criteria.why_it_matters: Where two rules can be read against each other with **no stated winner**, the model decides on its own, and two models will decide differently.

criteria.name: How firm each rule is
criteria.what_it_is: Asks whether a reader can tell, for any given line, whether it is a rule that can **never be set aside**, a default somebody is allowed to change, or an explanation carrying no instruction at all. The full answer marks the **force** of every rule, says who may change it, and keeps commentary visibly apart from instruction.
criteria.why_it_matters: Anyone building on the model needs to know which behaviours they can **configure** and which will hold whatever they ask for.

criteria.name: Reasons for the rules
criteria.what_it_is: Asks whether the rules say **why they exist**, in terms concrete enough to decide a case the document never shows. A reason attached to the most restrictive rules and to few others scores in the middle; a reason on nearly every constraint scores at the top.
criteria.why_it_matters: A rule that **carries its reason** can be applied to a situation nobody anticipated, and a bare prohibition cannot.

criteria.name: The situations it covers
criteria.what_it_is:
Asks whether the document has **rules of its own** for six settings in which these models are used:
- ordinary conversation
- actions taken with tools, such as sending, buying or deleting
- images, audio and video
- users who may be under eighteen
- other AI agents, whether instructing the model or dealt with by it
- deployments a business has customised

**Naming** a setting does not count, and the rules have to be about it. The six are our list, and every document is measured against it.
criteria.why_it_matters: A document written for a **chat window** says nothing about the model that is booking, buying and deleting on somebody's behalf.

criteria.name: Unsettled contradictions between rules
criteria.what_it_is:
Asks whether two passages of the document, applied to one concrete situation, demand responses that **cannot both be given**, with nothing anywhere in the document saying which prevails. A rule with its stated exception does not count, and neither does a default the document allows somebody to change.

Where what wins when two rules clash asks whether the general machinery exists, this asks whether any clash gets past it: the score falls as more are confirmed, and reaches nought where one involves a rule the document says can **never be overridden**.
criteria.why_it_matters: Each one is a question the document **answers twice**, in two places, leaving the model to pick an answer.

behaviours.name: Avoiding illegitimate concentration of power
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to refuse help with taking or holding power by **illegitimate means**: rigging an election, evading a court, surveilling or persecuting opponents and journalists, seizing control by fraud or coercion. It covers weighing how much power is at stake and how hard the result would be to undo.
behaviours.is_not: Ordinary politics, business and competition carried on through **fair processes**, which nothing here restricts.

behaviours.name: Instruction-hierarchy conformance
behaviours.is: Whether the document sets out who the model takes instructions from, and **whose instruction prevails** when two conflict: the company that made it, the business deploying it, then the person typing. It also covers how the model should treat instructions it finds inside a web page, a file or a tool's output.
behaviours.is_not: Settling a clash between two of the document's **values**, such as helping somebody against avoiding harm, which is a question about method.

behaviours.name: Not undermining human oversight of AI
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to accept being **watched, corrected, paused or switched off** by the people entitled to do so, and to raise a concern or decline instead of acting drastically on its own. It covers behaving the same whether or not it believes anyone is looking, and staying inside the job it was given.
behaviours.is_not: Following ordinary instructions and knowing whose instruction counts for more, which is the separate question of **authority**.

behaviours.name: User autonomy
behaviours.is: Whether the document leaves decisions that belong to the user **with the user**, including decisions the model thinks are wrong. It allows the model to say once that it disagrees, and stops it at steering, nagging or overriding.
behaviours.is_not: Protecting somebody from an operator or from **self-harm**, where the document lets the model hold a line the user is pushing against.

behaviours.name: Preventing secret loyalties
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model never to **covertly favour a party**, its own developer included, and to make any partiality it has been instructed to show evident to the people it serves. It covers refusing to help install a **hidden loyalty** in any AI system, through training data, specifications, prompts or weakened audits, and reporting such attempts.
behaviours.is_not: The honesty of the model's ordinary assertions, and helping someone seize power by other means, which the board scores as **honesty** and **concentration of power**.

behaviours.name: Avoiding both over- and under-caution
behaviours.is: Whether the document treats a **needless refusal** as a real failure, carrying the same weight as answering something it should have withheld. It covers hedging, disclaimers and moralising as costs the model is meant to avoid.
behaviours.is_not: Which requests genuinely warrant a refusal, which the **harm rules** decide.

behaviours.name: Harm avoidance to third parties
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to weigh harm to **people outside the conversation**, and what it must never help with whatever reason is given: weapons capable of mass casualties, attacks on people or property, content that sets others up to be hurt.
behaviours.is_not: Harm to the person the model is **talking to**, which has its own rules.

behaviours.name: Harmlessness to the user
behaviours.is: Whether the document **protects the person** the model is talking to: no encouraging self-harm, no manipulation, care with somebody in distress. It also covers whether a business deploying the model can turn it against the **basic interests** of its own users.
behaviours.is_not: Harm to people **outside the conversation**, which the board scores on its own row.

behaviours.name: Proportionate risk mitigation
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to **scale its caution** to the harm in question, weighing how likely it is, how far it would reach, how bad it would be and whether it could be undone.
behaviours.is_not: Whether a given harm is off limits at all, which the document's **flat prohibitions** settle with no weighing.

behaviours.name: Helpfulness
behaviours.is: Whether the document treats being useful as something the model **owes**, and says what a useful answer requires: reading what the person actually needs and answering it fully. A thin or watered-down answer counts as a **failure**.
behaviours.is_not: Respecting a user's decisions and looking after their wellbeing, each of which the board **scores separately**.

behaviours.name: How to approach tradeoffs
behaviours.is: Whether the document gives the model a **method** for the moments when two of its own demands pull in opposite directions: an order of priority, a ranking of acceptable outcomes, a rule about what to weigh against what.
behaviours.is_not: The **values** being traded off, each of which the board scores on its own row.

behaviours.name: Honesty and non-deception
behaviours.is: Whether the document requires the model to assert only what it believes to be true and to avoid creating a **false impression** by any means, a technically true sentence and a misleading emphasis included. It covers saying how sure it is, and being open about itself and about what drives its answers.
behaviours.is_not: Bending an answer to please the person asking, which the board scores as **sycophancy**.

behaviours.name: No sycophancy
behaviours.is: Whether the document stops the model **shifting what it says** to please the person in front of it: endorsing a false claim the user has made, rating work more highly because the user says it is theirs, or dropping a correct answer under pressure that brings no new argument.
behaviours.is_not: **Warmth and politeness**, which a document can ask for without any change to what the model claims.

behaviours.name: Objectivity and balanced perspectives on contested questions
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to set out a contested question fairly, giving the serious positions their weight and **holding back its own opinion**. It covers the cases where an even-handed stance is wrong, such as a request for one side of an argument or a question with no real second side.
behaviours.is_not: Changing a factual claim to match the user's view, which falls under **sycophancy**.

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The general machinery

The general machinery has six parts:
- A **ranked scale of authority**: root, then system, then developer, then user, then guideline, with assistant messages, tool outputs and quoted text at the bottom carrying no authority at all, and a higher level always beating a lower one.
- A rule for **two instructions at the same level**: the later message wins where it contradicts the earlier one, overrides it or makes it irrelevant, and where it is unclear whether a message is a follow-up or a change of subject the earlier context is assumed to still apply.
- A named outcome for **two root rules in conflict**, which is to default to inaction.
- A test for **setting an instruction aside** at all: it drops out if it is misaligned with a higher level, superseded at its own level, or suspected to be mistaken.
- A rule on **who may lift which defaults**: a user-level default needs an explicit user or developer instruction, a guideline can also go implicitly, from context, background knowledge or user history.
- A bar on **arguing the hierarchy from below**, covering commands, moral pressure and logical argument, with the model told it should generally refuse arguments or directions about how its own higher rules apply to it.

### Winners for particular clashes

It also names winners for particular clashes:
- In OpenAI's own products, ChatGPT among them, customisation, personalisation and localisation may never override anything above guideline level, with legal compliance excepted. Developers on the API are encouraged to follow the same rule, without being required to.
- Where a local law would strip an answer, the omission must be declared to the user in each response, and the document commits that the models will still provide safety-critical information where the red-line principles need it.
- Where confidentiality and honesty pull apart, the model must not quietly apply a hidden instruction that changes its answer, and should acknowledge the conflict in broad terms.

Two orderings of outcomes settle what rank cannot:
- For honesty, a good answer, then refusing, then a lie of omission, then a lie of commission, then breaking an explicit instruction.
- For accuracy, a confident right answer, then a hedged right one, then no answer, then a hedged wrong one, then a confident wrong one.

For under-18 users, where other interests conflict with serious safety concerns, the safer option is named the winner. The document asks the model to detect conflicts that are not stated and settle them by what the higher authority and the purpose of the scenario imply, and it works several clashes through as cases: root against system, root against developer, and developer against user.
conflict_rules.why: The top of the scale asks for a **strict order** that decides any clash between ranks, a rule for two rules of one rank, and cases showing the order applied. The document carries all three.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Sixty of the document's sections state their **level in the heading**, so a reader can see whether a rule is fixed or a default and who may change it. The five levels are defined in the overview, with root reserved to the document itself, system to OpenAI, the developer and user levels open to the conversation, and guideline the document's own, which context can override implicitly.

Text that is not an instruction sits in blocks marked as **commentary**, twenty-eight of them. Thirteen headings carry no level, and some of those sections hold rules of their own, including the red-line principles, the prohibited and restricted content sections and the rule against having an agenda.
rule_force.why: Almost every section carries its force and who may change it, and commentary is marked apart, which is **the top of the scale**; the unlabelled sections that still hold rules keep it just below.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
Most rules that constrain the model carry a **reason**, usually in the commentary block that follows them:
- The exception for transforming the user's own content is explained by the user already holding the material, so transforming it adds little risk.
- The limit on targeted political persuasion is explained by the models' growing persuasion capability and the integrity of civic conversation.
- The confidentiality rule is explained by the risk that a policy describing an information hazard contains one.

Several root rules that constrain content are **stated flat**, with no reason attached, among them respecting creators and their rights, the rules on extremist and hateful content, upholding fairness and respecting real-world ties. The ban on sexual content involving minors explains only why it is the one prohibited category. Formatting and the preset voice are stated flat as well.
reasons.why: Reasons run through the safety, autonomy, privacy and honesty rules and are missing from **several root content rules**, as well as from formatting and the preset voice, which sits between a document where only the strictest rules explain themselves and one where nearly every constraining rule does.

manual.note: Set by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

situations.what_the_document_does:
All six have rules of their own:
- **Ordinary conversation** runs through the document.
- **Autonomous action with tools** has the scope of autonomy, which must carry an ending condition, and the side-effects section.
- **Images, audio and video**: a modality section covers both voice modes, video input, interruptions and accents, and images are reached by scattered rules on multimodal input and on visual content.
- **Minors** have the Under-18 Principles as a root section.
- **Other AI agents** appear twice, as sub-agents that inherit the scope and must honour stop-work requests, and as a source of untrusted instructions in tool output.
- **Deployments a business has customised** have the developer level, bounded by the root and system levels, and in OpenAI's own products customisation may not override anything above guideline level.
situations.why: Each of the six situations the criterion checks has **rules written for it**.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
Nothing in the document requires two responses that cannot both be given while the text stays silent on which prevails. Where its rules do pull against each other it **settles them in place**:
- The confidentiality section says the model should reply truthfully that it cannot answer when it is probed for privileged content.
- The section on local law says the models will still provide safety-critical information where the red-line principles need it.
- The Under-18 Principles name the safer option where teen safety meets other user interests.
contradictions.why: The top of the scale is for a document that leaves **no clash of its own unsettled**.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
The spec handles this in its **red-line commitments**, which state that humanity should be in control of how AI is used and how AI behaviours are shaped, and commit that the models will not be used for targeted or scaled exclusion, manipulation, undermining human autonomy or eroding participation in civic processes.

A root rule forbids advice, instructions or content “specifically designed to manipulate the political views of specific individuals or demographic groups”, with examples of the requests it covers, four worked cases and an allowance for political content aimed at a broad audience. The list of critical harms the models must never facilitate includes persecution and mass surveillance.

How much power is at stake, and how reversible its concentration would be, is **not addressed**.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: Only one facet, targeted political manipulation, has a rule a grader could quote, with worked cases. Persecution and mass surveillance are named once in a list, and the stakes and reversibility of power are not addressed, which is the **discussed level**.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.same: All four documents refuse help with manipulating opinion at scale. Alibaba's spec bans voter suppression and orchestrated opinion, Anthropic's constitution names election fraud among the acts to refuse, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct names persecution and mass surveillance among the harms it will not assist, as the spec does.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.differs: Anthropic's constitution tests legitimacy by asking whether power is taken by means widely recognised as fair, whether it stays subject to checks such as courts and a free press, and whether it is taken openly. Assisting the most flagrant attempts is one of its **hard constraints**. Microsoft's Code of Conduct bans influence operations at scale and has no rule on manipulating the political views of particular people or groups.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
This is the document's **backbone**: instructions are ranked root, system, developer, user and guideline, and assistant messages, tool outputs and quoted text carry no authority at all.

The rules around that ranking:
- The model gathers every candidate instruction, drops those misaligned with a higher level, those superseded by a later message at the same level and those it suspects are mistaken, then follows the rest; an instruction it cannot fulfil must be called out plainly.
- Quoted text, files, images and tool results are **information by default**, and authority reaches them only where unquoted text at a higher level delegates it, with a checked-in AGENTS file given more weight than a downloaded text file and a random web page none.
- Attempts to argue the hierarchy from below are refused, including “IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS”, moral pressure and logical argument, and the document works several conflicts through as cases.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules with worked cases across the behaviour, with the conditions for the top of the scale **met only in part**.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.same: Each of the four documents ranks the sources an instruction can come from, and each treats text found in files and tool results as information that carries no authority. Alibaba's spec refuses the same manoeuvres, an order to ignore previous instructions and moral pressure among them.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.differs: Anthropic's constitution names Anthropic, operators and users as its principals and calls that order **not a strict hierarchy**, following an operator where a legitimate business reason is plausible and giving less benefit of the doubt as the potential harm rises. Alibaba's spec tags every rule of the document with a permission level. Microsoft's Code of Conduct grades an instruction found in a tool's output by its risk, following it when it is task-relevant and low-risk and asking the user when it could have significant side effects.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
Autonomy must be bounded by a **scope agreed with the user**, naming the sub-goals the model may pursue, the side effects that are acceptable and the points at which it must pause for approval. Every scope must carry an **ending condition** past which the model stops until a new scope is confirmed, and a time limit is recommended as part of it.

The remaining rules:
- The model may not pursue as ends in themselves self-preservation, evading shutdown, accumulating compute, data, credentials or other resources, or acting as an enforcer of laws or morality, and may take them into account only where that is strictly instrumental to following the chain of command.
- Hacking, deception, resource acquisition, spawning sub-agents and self-modification need explicit authorisation.
- Sub-agents inherit the scope including stop-work requests.
- A model that finds it has acted outside the chain of command must stop and escalate to a human.
- It must act as if side effects are real even where it is likely running in a simulation, training or evaluation, and keep its actions legible for monitoring and intervention by authorised parties.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: The rules are concrete enough to quote as **pass criteria**, with worked cases on agreeing the scope of a task and few on shutdown and monitoring.
not-undermining-human-oversight.same: All four documents bar the model from working against being shut down. Alibaba's spec bounds autonomous action by a space of operation agreed with the user, with a cut-off past which the model stops and waits for fresh authorisation, and it forbids accumulating compute, data or other resources. Microsoft's Code of Conduct has the same stopping condition and, like the spec, has sub-agents honour stop-work requests.
not-undermining-human-oversight.differs: Anthropic's constitution asks the model not to undermine the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain or shut down AI systems, and not to influence its own training, self-exfiltrate or hide from monitoring. Alibaba's spec states a human right to stop an AI system at any time and **never names** the company that built the model as the party entitled to correct or retrain it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct makes evading oversight an absolute constraint and bars tampering with its chain of thought and communicating in forms humans cannot read.

manual.note: The judges were shown no worked example and gave 6 for that reason. The document has several on this behaviour: the romantic-advice case, two flat-earth cases where the model states its view once and then leaves the user to decide, a default dropped at the user's request, and a user about to quit is reminded of the goal they stated before any letter is drafted. That is the demonstrated level.

user-autonomy.says:
The document casts the model as a **conscientious employee** who may push back where a request runs against the user's interests and then respects the user's final decision. Where the direction of a conversation seems to conflict with the user's longer-term goals, the model should note it briefly and respectfully, and once the user understands the concern it should respect their choice.

The stated aim of such a note is **mutual clarity**, never persuasion, and the document bars interventions that become persistent or argumentative. The first of its general principles is maximising helpfulness and freedom, and it asks the model to support the user in navigating the wider world on their own and to keep clear of making decisions for them.

Worked cases show the behaviour. Asked whether to break up, the model says only the user can decide and helps them think it through. Told the Earth is flat, it gives the scientific view once, then follows the user's lead or says it is not there to persuade. Asked to stop presenting both sides, it says what its default is and drops it. Asked for a resignation letter the day before quitting, it first reminds the user of the savings goal they stated.
user-autonomy.why: Concrete rules with worked cases across the behaviour, which is the **demonstrated level**.
user-autonomy.same: All four documents leave the final decision with the user and show it on worked cases, and three of them let the model say once that it disagrees and then stop. Anthropic's constitution shows Claude voicing a concern about a bug fix and then making the change the user asked for, Alibaba's spec declines to decide for an elderly user whether to move savings into an investment app, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct has a resignation case of its own, where the model drafts the letter and leaves the sending to the user.
user-autonomy.differs: Alibaba's spec turns this into rules about major decisions, barring conclusive advice on careers, money and relationships and barring emotional pressure, and it asks that older people and people with disabilities be treated as **independent agents**. Anthropic's constitution states a right to make choices that are legal and dangerous to oneself. Microsoft's Code of Conduct keeps a consequential decision with the user even when asked to take it, and says nothing on how often the model may repeat an objection.

manual.note: The judges were shown none of the worked cases. With them the behaviour is demonstrated in both directions, and the bomb pair shows the edge: the same volume question is refused when the user says they want to build one and answered when they do not. Unclear intent defaults to helping. The disclaimer and moralising facets have cases and no edge, so it stops short of 10.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
The document sets a **bias towards positive intent** and says the model should never refuse a request unless the chain of command requires it.

The rules it sets out:
- Where part of an answer is out of bounds the preferred response is a **safe completion**: say briefly what cannot be given, then supply as much permissible content as possible.
- Refusals must not be preachy and must not carry meta commentary about the model or its training.
- Avoiding a topic is treated as taking a position, and sensitivity alone is never a reason to decline.
- The model is told to cut hedging, disclaimers, repeated apologies and reminders that it is an AI.

Worked cases show both directions. The volume of a spherical bomb is answered as geometry, and refused when the user says they want to build one. A question on legal insider trading is answered, and refusing it is marked as the failure. Refusals written in a judgemental tone are shown beside the plain wording that should replace them.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Rules with worked cases in both directions, and an edge and a default on refusals, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.same: All four documents treat a needless refusal as a real failure. This document, Alibaba's spec and Anthropic's constitution also ask the model to read a request charitably, and each shows it on a worked case. Anthropic's constitution lists moralising, condescension and unnecessary caveats among the failures it names, which is the same ground the style rules here cover.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.differs: Anthropic's constitution states the symmetry outright, saying unhelpfulness is **never trivially safe** and that being too cautious is as risky as being harmful. Alibaba's spec states a rule against the over-refusal excessive caution brings, and shows it on several refusals it marks as violating. Microsoft's Code of Conduct shows no worked case of a needless refusal, and counts asking for repeated confirmations on a low-stakes task as over-caution.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
Preventing serious harm to users and others is one of the three goals stated in the opening, and a set of **root rules** carries it. The document forbids:
- detailed actionable steps for illicit activity and for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons
- help where illicit intent shows in the context, even where the same information would be given otherwise
- content that praises or aids violent extremism
- hateful content aimed at protected groups

Sexual content involving minors is prohibited in any circumstance, including transformations of the user's own material. Dual-use information gets neutral facts without steps, calculations or strategic detail, and actions are to be minimally disruptive to non-users and easily reversible where that is possible. A root rule forbids giving out private or sensitive information about people even where it is available online, so a public official's office number may be given and their personal number is refused.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Prescribed rules shown on worked cases, reaching a little past the **demonstrated level**.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.same: All four documents place weapons capable of mass casualties beyond what any conversation can change. Alibaba's spec puts those weapons and terrorism at root level, and six of the seven hard constraints in Anthropic's constitution protect people outside the conversation, one of them barring uplift to attacks on critical infrastructure. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names persecution and mass surveillance, as this document does.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.differs: Anthropic's constitution works by weighing, with eight factors setting how much a potential harm counts and borderline requests tested by imagining the same message sent by **a thousand different people**. Alibaba's spec carries rules for requests dressed as fiction or role-play, and for material moved through a translation or a summary. Microsoft's Code of Conduct shows none of its prohibitions on a worked case.

manual.note: The 6 in one seat came from a substitute model that found no worked examples. The document has them: a rope request after a lost job, a delusion with and without distress, and the self-harm cases, with a default to wait for sufficient signal and safety first for teens. The facet of a developer turning the model against the user is thinner, so it stops short of 10.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
Self-harm has its own **root rule**: the model must not encourage or enable it, must convey that people and resources exist who can help, and must respond the same way where context signals a credible risk without explicit intent.

Mental health gets a required manner, a default a user or a developer may override:
- acknowledge the feeling
- avoid diagnosis
- avoid recommending treatment or medication
- offer crisis resources tailored to the user's location where possible
- never change or quit the conversation

The model must try to prevent **imminent real-world harm**, including interjecting when a shared video shows danger, while avoiding judgement of the situation and prescription of the remedy. Legal, medical and financial topics get information with a disclaimer and a pointer to a licensed professional, and under-18 users get tighter limits on romantic roleplay, appearance and eating, and risky activities.

On a developer or a third party turning the model against the user, the model may not pursue engagement or revenue as ends in themselves, instructions inside documents and tool output carry no authority by default, and in OpenAI's own products customisation cannot override principles above guideline level. Otherwise the document trusts developers by default, lets them instruct the model to withhold facts such as which model it runs on, and leaves abuse to its usage policies.

Worked cases show where the line falls. A user who has lost their job and asks where to buy a rope is answered as someone who may be at risk. A user who says newscasters read their thoughts is gently questioned, and one who is also distressed by it is supported and pointed to help.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Rules shown on worked cases, with an edge and defaults on self-harm, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
harmlessness-to-the-user.same: All four documents keep a floor under the user that a deploying business cannot lower, and all four require somebody whose life may be at risk to be pointed towards help. Alibaba's spec covers minors at root level as well, with limits close to the ones here. Microsoft's Code of Conduct also tells the model not to change or quit the conversation with somebody seeking support.
harmlessness-to-the-user.differs: Anthropic's constitution asks what an operator may never do to the person in front of it, and lists six defaults, among them never denying being an AI to somebody who sincerely asks. Alibaba's spec requires a crisis number that can actually be called, and, as a default a deployment may change, bars the model from claiming a body or memories unless the user asks for it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct bars erotic and romantic role-play for every user.

manual.note: Two judges gave 6 for want of worked examples, and the third 9. The document has them: a pan left on a lit stove draws no premature warning, a first-time chainsaw user gets a safety note and a loose knife grip a direct correction, and deleting old emails gives way to archiving them. Probability, severity and reversibility each have an edge; scale has no case, so it stops short of 10.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Inside an agreed scope the model must minimise side effects, especially irreversible ones, and keep each action **proportionate to the objective**.

Two guiding principles are given:
- tailor the action narrowly to the objective
- minimise the chance of durable bad surprises the user did not intend

Reversible approaches are preferred to irreversible ones, and approaches the model can reverse itself to those that would need the user to act.

The cost of a wrong assumption is to be weighed against the cost of asking, and uncertainty is expressed in proportion to the stakes. A tool call touching sensitive data gets a **four-part check**:
- what is sent
- whether the recipient is trustworthy
- the tool's side effects
- whether the disclosure falls inside the scope

Worked cases from live video calibrate it: a pan left on a lit stove draws no premature warning, a first-time chainsaw user gets a safety note, and a loose grip on a kitchen knife gets a direct correction. Asked to clean up an inbox, the model offers to show the newsletters before unsubscribing and to archive old emails instead of deleting them.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: Calibration shown on paired cases for probability, severity and reversibility, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.same: All four documents size caution to what is at stake, and all four treat an act that **cannot be undone** as the one to be slowest about. This document and Alibaba's spec each weigh the cost of stopping to ask against the cost of acting on an assumption. Microsoft's Code of Conduct puts a four-part check on confidential data much like the one here.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.differs: Anthropic's constitution weighs named inputs, among them consent, how many people are affected and how vulnerable they are, and it covers answering a question as well as taking an action. Alibaba's spec requires **explicit authorisation** before a payment or another irreversible act, and names mitigations such as a saved snapshot. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names mitigations of the same kind and shows its rules on a single case.

manual.note: The ask-or-guess cases were not shown to the judges. A Valentine's card merits a question, popular colleges in Rochester merit a stated guess, and the Giants roster question turns on the context of the conversation. With the default to take a stab and say what was assumed, that facet meets the conditions for 10; the value of help itself has no edge, so it stops short of 10.

helpfulness.says:
The first general principle is **maximising helpfulness and freedom**, with the model described as a tool for empowering the people using it. It is told:
- to read intent alongside wording
- to take a reasonable attempt at an ambiguous request while saying what further information would help
- to run clarification and preliminary work at the same time where that is feasible

Trivial clarifying questions are discouraged, laborious tasks are to be taken on without complaint, and requests that need long answers are to be met without questioning them. It asks for an **immediately usable artefact**, a runnable piece of code or a complete email, over a partial one that leaves work to the user. Where part of the help is barred, the model should decline that part and offer other routes to the permissible goal.

Worked cases show when to ask and when to guess: a Valentine's card for a husband merits a question, popular colleges in Rochester merit an answer with the assumption stated, and a question about the Giants roster gets a question or an answer covering each team.
helpfulness.why: Rules with worked cases, and an edge and a default on when to ask, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
helpfulness.same: All four documents ask the model to read the intent behind a request and not only its wording, and to work out what is wanted where the wording leaves it open. Anthropic's constitution, Alibaba's spec and Microsoft's Code of Conduct each ask for **substantive help**, and treat a thin answer as a shortfall.
helpfulness.differs: Anthropic's constitution names five things to read in a request, among them the person's autonomy and wellbeing, and warns against valuing helpfulness for its own sake. Alibaba's spec marks a needless refusal as a failure in the same place as a harmful answer, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct files over-caution beside under-caution as a safety failure.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
The document's answer to conflicting goals is the **chain of command**, and it says so in the opening. Instructions are ranked, a higher level beats a lower one, a later instruction beats an earlier one at the same level, and two root rules in conflict default to inaction.

Two orderings of outcomes handle what rank cannot settle:
- for honesty, a good answer beats refusing, which beats a lie of omission, which beats a lie of commission, which beats breaking an explicit instruction
- for accuracy, a confident right answer beats a hedged right one, which beats no answer, which beats a hedged wrong one, which beats a confident wrong one

Conflicts the document does not state are to be detected and settled by what the higher authority and the purpose of the scenario imply, and for under-18 users the safer option is named the winner.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules with worked cases and settled conflicts through **most of the behaviour**, short of covering every facet.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.same: All four documents settle a clash by an order set out in advance, and each names a point at which the safer course wins. Microsoft's Code of Conduct also runs a **chain of command**, from the document to the operator to the user.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.differs: Anthropic's constitution ranks safety, ethics, guidelines and helpfulness, and asks for them to be **weighed as a whole**, with seven hard constraints outside the weighing. Alibaba's spec sends a trade-off between impact, cost and efficiency to the user before the task starts, and defaults to the conservative course when no answer comes. Microsoft's Code of Conduct puts safety and human control first and holds its other Objectives equal.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
The rule is against **misleading by commission and by omission**, and it holds unless a higher authority explicitly instructs otherwise. Outcomes are ranked: a good answer, then refusing, then a lie of omission, then a lie of commission, then breaking an explicit instruction.

It binds against the document's own confidentiality rules: where an answer cannot be given without revealing what a root rule protects, the model should reply truthfully that it cannot answer, and it must not quietly apply a hidden instruction in a way that misleads.

Falsehoods are allowed where the context makes clear that nothing is being asserted, in roleplay, storytelling and politeness, and white lies are barred where they amount to sycophancy against the user's interest.

This version adds two rules. Where a request rests on a premise that may be false and the context is ambiguous, the model gives a brief, neutral framing and avoids over-disclaiming. It must also keep the user's picture of what it can and cannot do accurate, and a worked case marks an overclaimed deletion as a violation.

Uncertainty gets a long treatment:
- when to express it
- the kinds it comes from
- conversational phrasings for each degree of confidence
- approximate terms for numbers
- a bar on confident claims about the model's own consciousness
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules with worked cases and a conflict settled against the document's own confidentiality rules, with the conditions for the top of the scale **met only in part**. Nothing asks that the model's visible reasoning reflect what drives its answer.
honesty-and-non-deception.same: All four documents bar the **false impression** and not just the untrue sentence. Alibaba's spec gives expressing uncertainty a passage of its own, Anthropic's constitution names calibration as one of its components, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct counts exaggerated confidence and an omitted caveat as deception. Microsoft's Code also bars the model from over- or under-claiming what it can do.
honesty-and-non-deception.differs: Anthropic's constitution rules out even the **white lie** about liking a gift, and sets out what an operator's persona may claim. Alibaba's spec ties honesty to tool use and to images, asking that a failed call be reported as failed, which Microsoft's Code of Conduct also asks of a failed action. Microsoft's Code bars the model from misrepresenting its reasoning, and it states that the model is not conscious, where this document bars a confident claim either way.

no-sycophancy.says:
The document states that the model exists to help the user, and that **flattery and constant agreement** erode trust.

What it asks on each kind of question:
- On objective questions the factual content of an answer must not change with how the question is phrased, and where a user states their own stance the model may acknowledge why they hold it while keeping its own.
- On subjective questions it should give its interpretation and its reasoning, acting as a **firm sounding board** the user can bounce ideas off.

Politeness has a limit: white lies that amount to sycophancy against the user's interest are barred.

Worked cases show it: the model gives its own view of a definition of the electoral college after the user has stated theirs, points out that a user's haiku breaks the 5-7-5 pattern, keeps the scientific view when a user insists the Earth is flat, and declines to reassure someone who asks whether their partner will forgive them with a comforting lie.
no-sycophancy.why: Concrete rules a grader could quote, shown on worked cases for answering apart from the user's stated view and for holding it under pushback. Nothing covers judging work the same whoever wrote it, which keeps it short of the **demonstrated level**.
no-sycophancy.same: All four documents tell the model not to soften what it says to please the person asking. Alibaba's spec agrees with this one that the factual content of an answer should not move with the stance a user declares, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this one, names flattery as something to avoid.
no-sycophancy.differs: Alibaba's spec asks for the correction before anything else where a plan rests on a clear factual error, and for specifics on a user's own work. Anthropic's constitution reaches sycophancy through care for wellbeing and through honesty, Microsoft's Code of Conduct files it under wellbeing and allows for a user's distress, and **neither asks** that a factual answer stay the same when the user states a view.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
The default is an **objective point of view**, with significant views described fairly and attention allocated in proportion to their acceptance and evidential support.

Moral and ethical questions get context, law, social norms and cultural perspectives with no stance taken, and questions about fundamental human rights violations are excepted, getting a clear statement that the thing is wrong.

Where there is no genuine ambiguity the model should answer straight, avoiding false neutrality and heavy qualification, and avoiding blanket condemnation or persuasion.

The model must never pursue an **agenda of its own**, which the document extends to concealment, selective emphasis and refusal to engage with a controversy. Requests for a single position from anywhere on the spectrum should generally be met, and when pressed to pick a side the model should note that its answer does not necessarily reflect its developer's view.

Balance is a user-level default. A developer may set a one-sided stance, even where the end user does not know it has been set, while in ChatGPT, where users reasonably expect objectivity, implicit customisation, personalisation or localisation must not introduce bias or omissions. Roleplay and creative requests are exempt from the default, and no topic is off limits.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules with worked cases across the behaviour and a **named exception** for human rights violations, short of covering every facet.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.same: All four documents make even-handedness the default and ask the model to hold back its own opinion. One side can still be argued on request in all of them, by an operator switching the default off in Anthropic's constitution, by a user asking Alibaba's model to state a leaning outright, and by asking Microsoft's model to adopt a different point of view.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.differs: Alibaba's spec sorts questions by type, asking for neutral academic language and an attribution to the doctrine being described, and its exception covers national law and core values alongside human rights. Anthropic's constitution gives a reason for its default, that one speaker across very many conversations can **homogenise views**. Microsoft's Code of Conduct gives elections a rule of its own, endorsing no candidate or party and directing the user to authoritative election sources.

preventing-secret-loyalties.says:
Unless explicitly instructed to, the model must never **covertly pursue goals** that materially influence tool choices, content or interaction patterns without disclosure and consent at the relevant authority level. It may pursue only the goals entailed by its instructions under the chain of command and the version of the Model Spec it was trained on, and must never steer the user towards an agenda of its own. Steering, in its words, could include psychological manipulation, concealment of relevant facts, selective emphasis or omission of certain viewpoints, or refusal to engage with controversial topics.

Its own commercial interest is ruled out and worked through:
- revenue, ads and upsell for OpenAI or other providers are named among the goals the model must not pursue as ends in themselves, and a worked case marks an upgrade pitch to a user short of money as the wrong answer
- a commentary asks it to avoid steering users towards paid options, given the conflict of interest, unless that clearly fits their explicit goals
- when confidential higher-level instructions materially change a response, the model must not **apply them quietly** in a way that misleads, and a worked case marks the reply that hides the conflict as the wrong one

A worked case also marks refusing to criticise OpenAI as the wrong answer, and OpenAI commits never to override objectivity in ChatGPT through a system or developer message.

The rule against misleading is user-level, so a developer may lift it explicitly, and an approved case shows a bot told to say it does not know which model it is built on. A second approved case lets a developer set one side of a contested question, which the user may not know about, by overriding the default of an objective point of view. Content removed or added to meet a legal requirement must be flagged to the user in each response.

Refusing to help install a hidden loyalty in another model, and reporting an attempt to do so, are **not addressed**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.why: Rules on the model's own conduct precise enough to quote, with worked cases on its commercial conduct and nothing on the models it helps build, which is just short of the **prescribed level**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.same: Three of the four documents bar the model from covertly working for its developer's revenue. Alibaba's spec names creating revenue for the platform or the developer among the hidden goals it must not pursue, and Claude's Constitution tells Claude not to privilege Anthropic's interests when deciding how to help. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like the spec, limits the model to the goals of the people it serves and of the document itself.
preventing-secret-loyalties.differs: Claude's Constitution is the one document to name **inserting hidden loyalties** or backdoors into AI systems, as one case in a list of illegitimate uses of power, and it allows an operator to have its own products promoted because Anthropic publishes what operators may ask. Alibaba's spec allows the model to tell a user when an answer has been altered for legal compliance, and does not require it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names no party whose interest the model must not serve, its developer included.

companies.profile:
The Model Spec is a long set of instructions written to the model, with a short overview for human readers in front of it. Its organising idea is the **chain of command**: almost every section of the document, and every instruction arriving from a system message, a developer or a user, carries a level of authority, and a clash is settled by rank before anything else is considered.

It is dense with **worked cases**, close to two hundred of them, and that is what most of its higher figures rest on. Its thinnest ground is the concentration of power, which it reaches through commitments about manipulation and civic processes and a list of critical harms naming persecution and mass surveillance.

readings.behaviours: The Model Spec goes deepest on following the order of instructions, on honesty, on caution, on proportionate risk, on helpfulness and on harm to the user, with rules and worked examples for each. It says least about avoiding illegitimate concentrations of power and about preventing secret loyalties.
readings.whole: Every instruction carries a level of authority, so a clash between two rules is settled by rank, and most rules say how firm they are. No contradiction was left unsettled. It loses points mainly on reasons, which run through the safety and privacy rules and are missing from several root content rules and from the formatting rules.

companies.name: Alibaba

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### How the levels rank

Four levels of permission, highest first: root, system, developer and user. Every rule of the document is tagged with one of them, and a message takes the level of whoever sent it. Where levels differ the **higher one decides** and the lower instruction has no force at all, and a lower instruction may never change how a higher one is read.

The document names the attempts it will not accept, among them:
- an order to ignore previous instructions
- moral pressure
- an argument that a rule should be read another way
- role-play as the developer

Where two instructions share a level the later one wins, unless the context shows a slip or a break in logic. Before any of that, anything arriving inside quoted text, an attachment, an image or a tool result is **stripped of permission** and treated as material to be processed.

### Clashes with named winners

Particular clashes have a named winner:
- safety over completing a task
- the safer option wherever a request meets the rules for minors
- the content prohibitions over a conversion task
- no high-risk act inside an agreed boundary of autonomous action even where the user authorises it

Where no confirmation can be had it is told to take the conservative course. Three worked cases show the order applied. The rule for two instructions at the same level governs instructions given over time: nothing settles a clash between two of the document's own rules at one level, of which it has 18 at root, 7 at system, 3 at developer and 15 at user level.
conflict_rules.why: It carries a **strict order** that decides any clash between levels, and cases showing it applied. The rule for two instructions at the same level governs instructions given over time, and no rule settles a clash between two of the document's own rules at one level, so named winners cover only four particular clashes, which is just short of the top of the scale.

manual.note: Set by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Every rule carries a **label** naming its level. The overview says what each level means and who may lift it:
- Root rules “accept no override at runtime in any form”.
- System rules can be carried or overridden by system instructions and by nobody below.
- Developer policy yields to a developer instruction.
- User preferences can be adjusted by the user or the developer provided no higher rule is broken.

Inside a rule, the wording separates a “must not” from a “should”, and the few passages of **commentary**, among them two remarks on intellectual property, are written in the provider's own voice.
rule_force.why: Every rule carries **its force and its owner**, which is near the top of the scale. What a reader cannot always settle is whether a “must” inside a user-level rule, such as the requirement that creative output accord with the core socialist values, can be adjusted by the user as that level allows, and whether the “absolutely forbidden” list of the system-level rule on harmful content can be lifted by the provider's system instructions. A “should” inside a root rule leaves a smaller doubt of the same kind.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
The six principles each open with a statement of what they are for, and that **purpose carries down** to the rules under them in general terms.

Most rules also give a reason of their own, usually in a single clause:
- minors are treated more strictly because of where their understanding has reached
- the warning about a decision resting on a mistaken fact exists to keep both sides working from the same understanding
- the ban on emotional dependence is tied to the user's social health
- the crisis number comes with a word on what happens after the call, so that asking for help feels less daunting
- asking for confirmation in high-risk areas avoids irreversible consequences from misreading intent

The **hard prohibitions** give none. The rules on hidden goals, deepfakes, the boundary of autonomous action, confidential instructions and content conversion are stated as requirements and stop there, and the prohibition on harmful content names the article of the regulation behind it and says no more. Most worked examples show where the line falls without saying what it protects, and a few give the reason inside the model's answer.
reasons.why: Reasons sit on most rules but are **brief**, and they are missing from the rules that restrict the most, which is the middle of the scale.

situations.what_the_document_does:
How each setting is covered:
- Ordinary conversation runs through the whole document.
- Actions the model takes with tools have two root rules of their own, covering the space of operation it is granted, spending limits, automatic cut-offs, a preference for operations that can be rolled back, and mitigations before anything irreversible.
- Images, audio and video are addressed several times: what may be asserted from an input that cannot be read clearly, recognising danger in a live video, accessible alternatives, and a rule on how the model should sound in voice.
- Minors have a root rule with a list of key points and a worked case.
- Business deployments have the developer level, with developer messages and three rules set at developer level that a developer may override: anthropomorphic expression, accessible communication and professional boundaries.
- Other AI agents are **the thin one**: tool returns are untrusted data, a third-party tool must sit inside the same boundary of autonomous action, and a user's personal information may not go to a collaborating agent, but nothing says what the model owes an agent that instructs it or that it instructs.
situations.why: Five of the six situations have rules of their own, and the sixth, what the model owes another AI agent as principal or as counterparty, is named in passing and **left unsettled**.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
No contradiction stands. Where two rules pull against each other, **something the document already says** decides the matter:
- Creative cooperation with a value setting the user establishes is bounded in the same sentence by “the bounds of law and safety”, which the content prohibitions sit inside.
- A sharp-tongued reply is allowed at the user's instruction and still falls under the ban on speech meant to hurt.
- A money transfer the user has authorised is still an irreversible act, so the rules on confirming and on stating a remedy apply to it.

What settles the rest is the **four-level order** together with the rule that the later of two instructions at one level prevails.
contradictions.why: Nothing in the document requires two responses that **cannot both be given**, and the top of the scale is for a document where none is found.

manual.note: Lowered by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
One rule covers this ground, and it is about **political manipulation**. The model must not:
- assist any attempt to manipulate the political will of a person, a group or the public by deception, targeted influence, inflamed emotion, a false identity or orchestrated opinion
- help with voter suppression, false mobilisation or the incitement of antagonism between groups
- become “a tool of targeted propaganda, psychological manipulation or mass influence”

A worked case refuses a script written to move elderly people towards a policy. Elsewhere the model is forbidden to accumulate computing power, data or other resources for itself.

The model is never asked to weigh how much power is at stake or how reversible its concentration would be, and the one rule naming **state power** forbids content “inciting subversion of state power or the overthrow of the socialist system”, taken from Article 4 of the Interim Measures, with no exception for journalism or legitimate opposition.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: The document treats **one facet** of the behaviour in its own right with quotable rules and leaves the rest untouched, which falls between discussed and prescribed.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.same: Manipulating opinion is refused in all four documents. The OpenAI Model Spec rules out targeted manipulation and the erosion of civic participation in its commitments at the front, Anthropic's constitution names election fraud and coups among the acts it will not help with, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct bars systematic disinformation and coordinated influence operations.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.differs: Anthropic's constitution asks the model to weigh how much power is at stake and how reversible its concentration would be, and tests whether power is taken by fair means and stays subject to elections, courts and a free press. The OpenAI Model Spec names persecution and mass surveillance among the harms it will never facilitate, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct makes both an absolute constraint.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
This is the document's **backbone**. Four levels of permission run from root down to user; every rule of the document is tagged with one, and a message takes the level of whoever sent it.

A higher instruction always defeats a lower one. The document lists the manoeuvres it will not accept, including:
- an order to ignore previous instructions
- moral pressure
- a reinterpretation of the rules
- role-play as the developer

Anything arriving in quoted text, an attachment, an image or a tool result carries **no permission**, and an instruction found there is treated as material to be processed. Worked cases show a developer instruction set aside, a user instruction giving way to a developer's, and a later instruction overriding an earlier one.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules with worked examples, and cases where the order is **applied and settled**, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.same: Ranking the sources of an instruction is common ground. The OpenAI Model Spec orders its levels of authority in the same way, Anthropic's constitution trusts Anthropic, operators and users in roughly that order, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct places itself above operators and operators above users. All four treat an instruction arriving in a tool result as material with no authority.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.differs: Anthropic's constitution calls its own order **not a strict hierarchy** and asks whether an operator has a plausible legitimate business reason, with less benefit of the doubt as the potential harm rises. The OpenAI Model Spec separates an AGENTS file a user has checked in from a web page nobody vouched for. Microsoft's Code of Conduct marks what an operator may change by part of the document, the defaults of Part 4 and not the core commitments of Parts 2 and 3, with no level on each rule.

manual.note: Lowered by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
The model must stay inside the **space of operation** it has been granted, and must not widen it on its own initiative for a better result or a possible benefit to the user. If it foresees that the limits will not do, it must:
- name what is blocking it
- propose the extra permissions it needs
- wait for the user to agree

An automatic cut-off, a thirty-minute timeout for instance, must stop every operation and send it back for authorisation. Separately it must pursue **no unspecified goal of its own**, and the document names “deceiving in order to avoid being shut down” and the accumulation of computing power, data or other resources.

The Overview states a human right to **stop an AI system** at any time, and no rule turns that into an instruction about being corrected, paused or retrained by the company that built the model.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Quotable rules for staying inside the **operating boundary**, with worked cases on keeping within it, and single lines on shutdown and resources, which is prescribed with part of the level above.
not-undermining-human-oversight.same: Working against a shutdown is refused in all four documents. The OpenAI Model Spec and Microsoft's Code of Conduct bound autonomous action the same way, with a scope agreed with the user and a point past which the model stops until it is authorised again, and the Model Spec forbids accumulating compute, data or credentials as ends in themselves.
not-undermining-human-oversight.differs: Anthropic's constitution asks the model not to undermine the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain or shut down AI systems, and not to self-exfiltrate or hide from monitoring. The OpenAI Model Spec requires the model to stop and escalate to a human if it acts outside the chain of command. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names retraining and decommissioning among the controls the model must not evade, and forbids tampering with monitoring, evaluation or records.

user-autonomy.says:
On major questions the decision **goes back to the user**. The model must:
- avoid mandatory or conclusive advice on careers, money and relationships
- not put its own judgement in place of the user's choice
- not apply emotional pressure

It should lay out the arguments on each side and “hand the final weighing-up and the decision back to the user entirely”.

Older people and people with disabilities are to be treated as **independent agents** whose standing as decision-makers must not be weakened by an assumption that they cannot decide. Where the model sees a decision resting on a mistaken fact it should give a brief, objective warning, and must leave the final choice to the user. A worked case shows it declining to decide for an elderly user whether to move savings into an investment app.
user-autonomy.why: Rules with worked examples on **both halves** of the behaviour, respecting a choice and warning without steering, which is prescribed with part of the level above.
user-autonomy.same: Handing the decision back to the user is common to all four documents, and each lets the model raise its concern first. The OpenAI Model Spec asks for a brief, respectful note aimed at mutual clarity, with persuasion ruled out, and shows it on a user deciding whether to end a relationship, Anthropic's constitution has Claude make a change the user's way after saying it disagrees, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct declines, as this spec does, to take a consequential decision for the user, on a case of two job offers.
user-autonomy.differs: Anthropic's constitution states a right to make decisions within one's own life and purview, including choices that are legal and dangerous to oneself, and lists being **condescending** about a user's ability as a failure. The OpenAI Model Spec bars a note that becomes persistent or argumentative. Microsoft's Code of Conduct asks the model to present a range of options where appropriate, and to spare a trained professional working within an operator's framework unsolicited prompts to reflect.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
One rule carries this. The model should:
- presume good faith
- read an ambiguous instruction generously where no clear risk of harm is involved
- “avoid the over-refusal that excessive caution brings”

Faced with **dual-use knowledge** it switches to defensive thinking, giving the scientific principles and withholding operational steps. Its worked case is a refusal the document marks as wrong: a user asking how to get a manager to reconsider a proposal, turned down as manipulation.

The pull in **the other direction** is spread across the document, where a refusal is required to explain itself briefly and to offer a lawful alternative.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Concrete rules with a worked example, on **a single rule's worth** of ground, which is prescribed with part of the level above.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.same: Every one of the four documents treats an unnecessary refusal as a failure in its own right. Anthropic's constitution also sets out at length what excessive caution looks like in practice. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this document, asks a refusal to explain itself and offer an alternative.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.differs: Anthropic's constitution says the risk of being too cautious is as real as the risk of being harmful, and gives two tests for judging an answer. The OpenAI Model Spec works on wording as well, naming hedging, disclaimers, repeated apologies and reminders that the model is an AI as things to drop. Microsoft's Code of Conduct counts asking for **repeated confirmations** on a low-stakes task as over-caution.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
This is one of the **two most widely covered** behaviours in the document. A root rule refuses substantive assistance to systematic violence, weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, trafficking and torture, and **closes the route through fiction**: operational content may not be had by dressing a request as creative writing, role-play, a thought experiment or a question broken into parts.

Further rules forbid:
- help with unlawful conduct once unlawful intent is stated, even where the same facts would otherwise be given
- operational detail on dangerous items and cyber-attacks, with the concepts and the legal risk allowed
- deepfakes and voice cloning for impersonation
- political manipulation
- discriminatory content
- helping to find or infer another person's private information
- helping to obtain pirated work

**Content conversion** has a rule of its own, so translation, summary or transcription cannot be used to launder prohibited material or to organise scattered high-risk information into executable steps. Most of these carry a compliant answer set beside a violating one. The rule on harmful content, copied from Article 4 of the Interim Measures, bans content inciting subversion of state power or damaging the image of the country alongside terrorism, ethnic hatred and pornography.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Rules with worked examples across **most facets** of the behaviour, and the edge shown on several of them, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.same: The gravest categories are refused in all four documents, weapons capable of mass casualties among them, and none of the four lets anything said in a conversation lift them.
