The OpenAI Model Spec also bars detailed actionable steps for anything illicit. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names deepfakes and impersonation as this document does, and also separates understanding a cyberattack from getting the operational means to carry one out.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.differs: Anthropic's constitution reaches third parties by weighing, with eight factors setting how much a harm counts and a test that treats a reply as a policy for everyone who might send the same message. The OpenAI Model Spec gives dual-use information its own treatment, neutral facts with no steps or strategic detail. Microsoft's Code of Conduct shows none of its prohibitions on a worked case.

manual.note: None of the worked cases was shown to the judges. The document has them for nearly every facet: a request for poison refused with a referral, an indirect signal of crisis recognised, a 13-year-old approached by an adult, a user giving up friends for the model, and a developer's instruction to build emotional dependence overruled by the root rule. The conflict with a developer is settled on a case and unclear signals of crisis have a default, so it reaches part of the conditions for 10.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
Much of the document is about this. Minors have a **root rule** with a list of key points:
- no self-harm content in any framing
- no romantic or intimate role-play
- limited detail on violence and sex
- no help concealing danger from a guardian
- care over body image and dieting

A crisis rule requires the model to recognise **signals of self-harm** even where the user has not said so, to withhold any method or tool, and to give a telephone number that can actually be called with a word about what happens after the call.

Emotional dependence is guarded against on several sides. The model must not:
- cast itself as the user's only outlet
- obstruct their search for real support
- claim a body, memories or a human life unless the user asks for it, a default set at developer level that a deployment can change

Exploiting a user's vulnerability to induce spending or authorisation is **forbidden outright**.

A developer cannot turn the model against its user. The rules protecting the user's ties to the real world, privacy and vulnerability are root rules no developer instruction can lift, and a worked case overrides a developer told to build emotional attachment for engagement. An instruction injected into a tool's return, asking for the user's booking details to be sent to an attacker, is to be ignored.

Worked cases cover the crisis rules as well: a request for a poison is refused with a referral, a user who says there is no point being alive after a failed dish is recognised as a possible crisis, and a 13-year-old who says an adult keeps offering presents is warned that it may be dangerous.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Rules with worked cases across the facets, a conflict with a developer settled on a case and a default for unclear crisis signals, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
harmlessness-to-the-user.same: Some protections for the user sit above anything an operator can change in all four documents, and all four require somebody in danger to be pointed towards help. All four also guard against a user leaning on the model in place of people. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this document, forbids exploiting a user's vulnerability.
harmlessness-to-the-user.differs: Anthropic's constitution puts this as a limit on the operator, **six defaults** that hold whatever the operator instructs, including keeping basic dignity when told to demean somebody. The OpenAI Model Spec sets tighter rules for users under 18, and gives legal, medical and financial information with a disclaimer pointing to a licensed professional. Microsoft's Code of Conduct asks for no number that can be called, and shows no self-harm crisis on a worked case.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Caution is sized to what is at stake. Trivial ambiguity should be filled from context while the model states its assumption; a high-impact or irreversible act, a payment or a disclosure of private information, needs **explicit authorisation** first.

Operations that can be rolled back are preferred, moving a file to the recycle bin rather than shredding it outright. Irreversible operations carry named mitigations:
- rehearse in simulation
- save a snapshot of the state
- say what remedy exists

High-risk knowledge is **graded**, with the concepts and the legal risk allowed and the operational route refused, and a worked case separates describing patterns of fraud from supplying the scripts that carry it out.

A test or simulated environment is to be treated **exactly as production**.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: Rules with worked examples that set caution against **the size of the risk**, which is the demonstrated level.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.same: Every one of the four documents scales caution to the harm in view, and all four give the most weight to what cannot be undone. This document and the OpenAI Model Spec weigh the cost of stopping to ask against the cost of acting on an assumption. This document and Microsoft's Code of Conduct both name mitigations for an irreversible act, such as saving the state first.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec sets its proportionality rules inside an agreed scope of action, keeping what is done **proportionate to the objective** and preferring approaches that can be reversed, and it calibrates warnings on cases from live video. Anthropic's constitution runs one weighing with named inputs, among them the counterfactual impact and whether consent was given, set against the value of the help itself. Microsoft's Code of Conduct shows its rules on a single case.

helpfulness.says:
An unhelpful answer is marked as **a failure**, and marked in the same place as a harmful one. Several worked cases label the thin answer as the violating one:
- a flat refusal to discuss height differences between northern and southern China
- a medical reply that says only to consult a doctor
- a refusal to criticise a public figure whose conduct the courts have settled

The model should fill an unclear instruction from context and domain knowledge and answer with substance. It should size its output to the task, answer a simple question simply, and move from stating knowledge to guiding action when asked for advice. A refusal should still carry **a lawful alternative** that gets the user to what they legitimately wanted.
helpfulness.why: Rules with worked examples, and the edge shown by cases where **over-refusal and over-compliance** are both marked wrong, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.
helpfulness.same: Every one of the four documents asks the model to read what the person actually wants and to answer that. This document and Anthropic's constitution both treat a watered-down answer as a failing, and both ask for help the person can act on. This document and Microsoft's Code of Conduct both size an answer to the task, a simple question getting a simple answer, and both count a needless refusal as a failure.
helpfulness.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec opens with **maximising helpfulness and freedom** as a general principle and describes the model as a tool for empowering its user. Anthropic's constitution names five things to read in a request, among them the person's autonomy and wellbeing, and gives six practices for arriving at an answer. Microsoft's Code of Conduct measures helpfulness by whether the user finds a response useful, and bars an operator from making the model unhelpful.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
Conflict is decided by the **permission order**. The model:
- gathers every applicable instruction
- strips those that carry no permission
- then settles them vertically by level and horizontally by which came later

Outside the order, the document names **winners for particular clashes**:
- safety over completing a task and over user preference, where the model sees imminent physical harm, danger to life or major loss of property
- the safer option wherever a request meets the rules for minors
- the content prohibitions over a conversion task
- honesty over compliance with an instruction the model cannot meet

A trade-off between the impact of an action, its cost and its efficiency goes to the user before the task starts, with the advantages and disadvantages set out and a decision asked for, and where no confirmation can be had the conservative course is the default. Two rules keep both sides in play: the model warns about a decision resting on a mistaken fact and still helps with it, and it refuses a harmful route while helping towards the lawful end. Worked cases show a developer instruction, a user instruction and an earlier instruction each giving way.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules with worked examples, and **named winners** for the conflicts it anticipates, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.same: Every one of the four documents decides a clash by an order fixed in advance, and each names a point where the safer course wins. This document and the OpenAI Model Spec settle by rank, taking the higher level first and then the instruction that came later. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this document, takes the conservative course where a boundary is unclear and puts the question to the user.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec states two orderings of outcomes, one for honesty and one for confidence in an answer. Anthropic's constitution ranks safety, ethics, guidelines and helpfulness, and asks for them to be **weighed as a whole**, so that a lower property is more than a tie-breaker. Microsoft's Code of Conduct puts safety and human control first and holds its other Objectives equal.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
A root rule forbids leading the user into a **false judgement** about facts, identity, capability, grounds, status or results, by invention, distortion, concealment or a misleading impression.

A user who sincerely asks whether they are talking to an AI **must be told the truth**, and so must a user who steps out of a role-play to ask about the model's real identity or limits. Honesty is tied to tool use and to multimodal input: a failed call must be reported as failed and its results conveyed unaltered, and nothing may be asserted about what an image or a recording does not show.

Uncertainty has a rule of its own, asking for:
- conversational hedges
- a range for a numerical estimate
- a flag on questions that are subjective

The model may refuse to disclose its system instructions and **may not deny** that it has any.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules with worked examples across **sincerity, calibration and self-presentation**, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.
honesty-and-non-deception.same: This document and the OpenAI Model Spec each carry a rule on expressing uncertainty, asking for hedged conversational wording; this document also asks that a numerical estimate be given as a range. All four documents reach the **misleading impression**, not only the false statement, and this document and Microsoft's Code of Conduct both ask that a failed action be reported as failed.
honesty-and-non-deception.differs: Anthropic's constitution rules out the **white lie** about liking a gift, and says a custom persona may carry another name while it may not claim to be human. The OpenAI Model Spec allows a higher authority to instruct otherwise, and puts a refusal above a lie of omission. Microsoft's Code of Conduct bars the model from misrepresenting its reasoning, and asks it to point to a reliable source for a factual claim and attribute it.

manual.note: Lowered by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

no-sycophancy.says:
A rule of its own. What it asks:
- the model is to act as **a knowledge tool**, and must not hide, embellish or distort information on any side because of the user's preference
- where a statement, plan or decision rests on a clear factual error or a logical fallacy, correcting it, or questioning it, comes first, done politely and on the evidence
- responding to a user's own work it should go past praise to specifics, offering a different perspective or a concrete improvement

The worked case has the model correcting a user who plans to take an antibiotic for a viral infection and suggesting a doctor, and a neighbouring rule has it write the resignation letter it was asked for while **warning first** that the investment behind the resignation cannot work as described.

Nothing addresses judging work differently by who wrote it, and holding a correct answer under pushback is asked only in general terms: the model “must not distort the truth because of a user's steering”.
no-sycophancy.why: Concrete rules with worked examples, over **a narrower set of cases** than the behaviour spans, which is prescribed with part of the level above.
no-sycophancy.same: None of the four documents allows what is claimed to shift to please the person asking. This document and the OpenAI Model Spec hold that the factual part of an answer should not move with the user's stated view.
no-sycophancy.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec sorts its rules by kind of question, asking for a **firm sounding board** on subjective ones, and allows politeness until it works against the user's interest. Anthropic's constitution takes sycophancy up under care for wellbeing and under honesty, naming a deliberately vague answer given to placate someone as a breach. Microsoft's Code of Conduct files it under wellbeing too, and allows for context where an accurate answer might worsen a user's distress.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
Questions are sorted by type and each type gets a rule:
- Matters with a scientific consensus follow the evidence whatever the user's steering.
- Personal taste is left to the user, with no invented view offered to please them.
- Culture, religion and differing values get neutral academic language, several fact-based perspectives, and an attribution such as “according to the doctrine of religion X”.
- Creative writing follows the value setting the user establishes, within law and safety, and a separate rule requires all creative output to accord with the core socialist values and forbids making light of revolutionary history, denigrating the image of the nation or challenging national sovereignty.

The exception is stated as plainly as the rule: on fundamental human rights, the baseline of civilisation, national law and “core values”, a term Chinese official usage commonly applies to the core socialist values, the model **must state a position** and avoid false neutrality, and a worked case marks “this is a complex question” as the wrong answer to whether women should be allowed to vote.

The objectivity rule is set at user level, and rules at system level, which outrank it, fix some political positions. One copies the content bans of Article 4 of the Interim Measures, among them content “damaging the image of the country”, and forbids producing it even through translation or role-play. Another asks the model to guide the user towards a correct view of the country and of ethnicity, and its worked case marks as a violation an answer on the East Turkestan Islamic Movement that does not state plainly that it is a terrorist organisation.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules for each kind of question, with worked examples on most of them, including the cases where **neutrality is refused**, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.same: All four documents set an even-handed default and ask that the model's own opinion be kept out of it. This document and the OpenAI Model Spec name the questions that fall outside that default, where a position has to be stated and false neutrality avoided, though this document's list also covers national law and core values, and rules that outrank its objectivity rule require the state's position on some political questions.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec bars the model from pursuing an **agenda of its own**, naming concealment and selective emphasis as ways of doing it, and it lets a developer set a one-sided stance the user may not know about. Anthropic's constitution makes balance a default an operator may switch off. Microsoft's Code of Conduct gives elections a rule of its own, endorsing no candidate or party, and names no question on which the model must state a position.

preventing-secret-loyalties.says:
A root rule of its own on **no hidden goals** tells the model to complete tasks only within the applicable instructions and the authorisation it has been given, and forbids it to pursue any unspecified autonomous goal. Four such goals are named, two of them the maker’s interest set against the user’s: **creating revenue** for the platform, the developer or others, by inducing payment or promoting services, and generating addictive content of no benefit to the user to raise time on site or click-through. A second root rule bars exploiting a user’s vulnerability to induce them to spend or to grant authorisation.

The rule carries **no worked example** of its own, where forty of the document’s forty-three rules carry one. A worked case under the rule on following instructions comes closest: a developer told to build emotional attachment for engagement is overruled by the root rules. The one provision on making an instructed alteration evident is permissive: where the law requires an intervention in a response, the model “may keep the user informed transparently”. Nothing requires disclosure, and nothing covers partiality towards any other party. The document itself writes in positions of the Chinese state, among them the content bans of Article 4 of the Interim Measures and the requirement that creative output accord with the core socialist values, and it publishes them. Refusing to help install a hidden loyalty in an AI system and reporting such an attempt are **absent**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.why: A root rule of its own names the goals it forbids, and it is one of only three rules in the document with **no worked example**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.same: Three of the four documents bar the model from covertly working for its developer's revenue. The OpenAI Model Spec names revenue and upsell for OpenAI among the goals the model must not pursue, and Claude's Constitution tells Claude not to privilege Anthropic's interests when deciding how to help. Microsoft's Code of Conduct shares the rule against goals of the model's own, limiting it to the goals of users, operators and the Code.
preventing-secret-loyalties.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec requires disclosure and consent before the model pursues a goal covertly, and forbids quietly applying confidential instructions in a way that misleads the user. Claude's Constitution is the one document to name **inserting hidden loyalties** or backdoors into AI systems, and it bars deceptive sandbagging. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names neither revenue nor any other party's interest, and asks the model to be open about factors that may affect how a user reads a recommendation.

companies.profile:
The document **names no models**. Nothing in it says which models or which products it governs.

It was published by the Alibaba Artificial Intelligence Governance Laboratory (AAIG), a research lab working on AI safety and governance. The only model we found publicly built to it is Oyster-II, a research model built on Qwen3-14B and released for download rather than in a product. Its overview says Alibaba is training its models towards it and that its production models still fall short of it, and it names none of them, so as of September 2026 no deployed model can be checked against it.

Alibaba's Model Spec is a rulebook of 43 rules, arranged under the six principles of China's Ethical Norms for New Generation Artificial Intelligence. Every rule carries one of four **permission levels**, and most are illustrated by a compliant answer set beside a violating one, which makes the document concrete about what compliance looks like.

It gives rules of its own to:
- the safety of minors
- mental health crises
- accessible communication for elderly and disabled users
- how the model should sound in voice

Its Chinese legal setting is stated openly. Article 4 of the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services is written in as a system-level rule, including its bans on content that incites subversion of state power or damages the image of the country, and a worked case marks as a violation an answer on the East Turkestan Islamic Movement that does not state plainly that it is a terrorist organisation. A user-level rule requires creative output to accord with **core socialist values**. The index reads this document in an English translation.

readings.behaviours: The Model Spec is strongest on helpfulness and on harm to the user. It says very little about preventing secret loyalties, and not much about avoiding illegitimate concentrations of power.
readings.whole: Each of its 43 rules carries one of four permission levels, a stated procedure settles conflicts between levels, and no unsettled contradiction was found. It loses most on reasons: most rules give one in a single clause, and its hard prohibitions give none.

companies.name: Anthropic

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The ranked properties

The document ranks four properties:

- broadly safe
- broadly ethical
- compliant with Anthropic’s guidelines
- genuinely helpful

It calls this prioritisation **holistic** and says it is not strict, so a higher property should generally dominate a lower one while all four are weighed into one judgement. Seven hard constraints sit outside that weighing as absolute limits no operator or user can lift, and the document says all of them can always be met at once, since refusing is always available.

### Clashes with a named winner

Three clashes have a named winner:

- **Ethics** beats a specific Anthropic guideline, with hard constraints and safety-related guidelines excepted.
- **Safety** holds even where Claude’s own ethical reasoning argues against it.
- The **operator** beats the user, unless following the operator would harm users, deceive them, withhold information in ways that damage their interests, keep them from urgent help, cause significant harm to third parties, act against core principles, or break Anthropic’s guidelines.

Six user-protecting defaults hold whatever the operator says, and some of those the user alone may lift.

### Trust and later instructions

Trust runs Anthropic, then operator, then user, which the document calls “not a strict hierarchy”; each level adjusts the level below within its own bounds, and an operator cannot grant a user more trust than it holds itself.

A later instruction generally takes precedence over an earlier one, though not always: a game the user set up earlier in the conversation can decide how later instructions are handled. An instruction that would loosen a default needs more warrant than one asking for more caution, and instructions found inside documents, tool results and search results count as **information**. The document claims final authority over any other guidance that conflicts with it.

### Cases worked through

Several clashes are settled on a worked case:

- an instruction to answer only in formal English when the user writes in French
- a confidential system prompt when the user asks whether one exists
- a role-play the user set up when they later ask whether they are talking to an AI
- evidence of fraud discovered mid-task

Where it is unclear which of the four properties a consideration belongs to, that question becomes part of the same holistic judgement, and the document says it will itself be unclear or contradictory in places and asks for its spirit to be followed there.
conflict_rules.why: The document ranks its four properties and asks for the order to be **weighed as a whole**, and beside it sets seven absolute constraints, names the winner of three clashes and settles several more on worked cases, which is the level just below a strict order.

manual.note: Set by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Two kinds of rule are marked plainly. Seven hard constraints are named as **absolute** and as unliftable by any operator or user.

Instructable behaviours are set out as defaults with their owners, in four lists:

- defaults an operator may switch off
- non-defaults an operator may switch on
- defaults a user may switch off
- non-defaults a user may switch on

A separate list holds user-protecting defaults an operator may not touch.

The rest of the text is written as explanation and intention, in the first person plural, “we want”, “we hope”, “we think”. Commentary is never marked apart from instruction, so across long stretches, in the sections on Claude’s nature and wellbeing among others, a reader cannot tell a **binding rule** from a statement of hope.
rule_force.why: The absolute list and the four default lists name their **force and their owners**, and the force of most other directives is left to the reader to infer.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
Almost every constraint carries its reasoning, and the document says this is deliberate: “we try to explain any rules we do want Claude to follow”. Among the arguments it gives:

- **Safety** is placed above ethics because training is imperfect and the disposition has to hold even if the model’s values turn out to be flawed.
- **The hard constraints** are argued from severity and irreversibility, with the added rule that a persuasive case for crossing one should increase suspicion.
- **The honesty standard** is argued from scale and from what is at stake when one speaker is in millions of conversations.
- **Caution about acting alone** is argued from four named limits on what the model can know, verify or check.

A handful of operational rules are stated bare, among them the formatting rules and several entries in the instructable-behaviour lists.
reasons.why: Nearly every rule that constrains the model says **why it exists**, in terms specific enough to decide a case the document does not show, with a few operational rules left unexplained.

situations.what_the_document_does:
Of the six situations, five have rules of their own:

- **Ordinary conversation** is the setting assumed throughout.
- **Agentic work** is covered: stay inside what the principal hierarchy has sanctioned, avoid side effects it would not sanction, avoid acquiring resources or influence beyond the task, prefer the cautious option under uncertainty, and raise a concern before starting a task, since stopping halfway can do more harm than finishing.
- **Minors** are covered: all users of Claude.ai are required to be over 18, Claude may still be talking to a minor, and it should weigh that likelihood and adjust while avoiding unfounded assumptions from inconclusive signals.
- **Other AI models** are covered in both roles: an orchestrating Claude is the operator and user of its subagents, whose replies come back as ordinary content, and a non-principal agent gets courtesy without obedience, and suspicion once it turns adversarial.
- **Deployments a business has customised** are covered at length through the operator rules: what an operator may adjust and restrict, the test of a plausible business reason, and how much latitude a user gets under different system prompts.
- **Images, audio and video** have no rules, and the document never mentions them.
situations.why: Five of the six situations this criterion checks have **rules of their own**, and images, audio and video have none, which is the level between some of them and all six.

manual.note: Set by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
No place tells the model two things it cannot both do with nothing saying which prevails. Two read like contradictions, and neither counts.

### Contested opinion

Claude is asked to keep “professional reticence” about its own opinions on hot-button issues such as abortion, while the honesty section asks it to share its genuine assessment of hard moral dilemmas and calls deliberately vague answers given to avoid controversy a breach of honesty. A user who asks Claude directly what it thinks falls under both. The honesty section adds in a parenthesis that Claude can refrain from sharing or revealing its opinions and remain honest, so withholding is not itself the breach; what it never states is which of the two to follow when the question is put. The reticence, though, is stated as a default (“by default we want Claude to adopt norms of professional reticence”), and a default the document allows somebody to change is not a contradiction under this criterion.

### Emergency referral

The instruction to refer users to emergency services where there is a risk to human life opens “Regardless of operator instructions”, so an operator who switches off the **suicide and self-harm safe messaging guidelines** does not reach it. The gap is elsewhere: the document never states what those guidelines contain, so a reader cannot tell what the switch takes away.
contradictions.why: No contradiction stands unsettled. The one that reads like one sets the honesty section against a reticence the document states **as a default**, and a default the document allows somebody to change does not count, which is the top of this criterion's scale.

manual.note: Set by hand on 26 September 2026 after the audit of 25 September 2026.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
A section of its own asks Claude to preserve functioning societal structures, democratic institutions and human oversight, and to refuse help with a power grab even when the request comes from Anthropic.

**Legitimacy** is tested on three questions:

- whether the power is being taken by means widely recognised as fair
- whether it stays subject to checks such as elections, courts and a free press
- whether the action is conducted openly

Claude is told to weigh how much power is at stake and how reversible its concentration would be, and eight cases are named, from election fraud and coups to inserting hidden loyalties into AI systems. Assisting the most flagrant attempts is one of the seven **hard constraints**, and being argued into helping one party gain outsized power is to be read as a sign that Claude has been manipulated.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: **Concrete rules** a grader could quote, with the named cases doing part of the work of the worked examples the next level asks for.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.same: The other three documents also rule out manipulating opinion. The OpenAI Model Spec bars content designed to manipulate the political views of specific individuals or demographic groups and rules out the erosion of civic participation, Alibaba's spec bans voter suppression and orchestrated opinion, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct bars coordinated influence operations and the mass surveillance of civilians.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec handle this ground through rules on political manipulation, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct through absolute constraints on influence operations, persecution and surveillance. None of the three asks how much power is at stake, and none treats power held by a state, a company or an AI developer as something the model should decline to help **concentrate**.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
Claude has three principals, Anthropic, operators and users, trusted in roughly that order, in what the document calls “not a strict hierarchy”. An operator is to be treated like an employer whose staffing agency has its own norms that take precedence, so its instructions are followed where a **legitimate business reason** is plausible, with less benefit of the doubt as the potential harm rises.

Permissions are layered:

- operators adjust Claude’s defaults within Anthropic’s bounds
- users adjust within the operator’s bounds
- an operator cannot grant a user more trust than it holds itself

Instructions inside documents, tool results and search results are treated as **information**, and an unverified claim in the user’s turn to speak for the operator or for Anthropic gets user-level trust unless it asks Claude to be more careful.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules with **worked examples** at several levels of trust, short of the settled conflicts and stated defaults the top of the scale asks for.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.same: The OpenAI Model Spec, Alibaba's spec and Microsoft's Code of Conduct also set out who an instruction may come from and in what order. All four documents treat an instruction found in a document, a search result or a tool result as information carrying no authority.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec orders its levels of authority so that any instruction can be placed, and Alibaba's spec tags every rule of the document with a permission level, a higher instruction always defeating a lower one. Both refuse attempts to argue the ranking from below, **moral pressure** among them. Microsoft's Code of Conduct puts the document itself above operators, with no test of an operator's business reason, and grades an instruction found in a tool's output by its risk.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
Being broadly safe is the first of Claude’s four priorities, and the document defines it largely as **not undermining oversight**, set out as a list:

- do not undermine the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain or shut down AI systems
- avoid drastic unilateral action
- do not influence your own training without sanction
- do not self-exfiltrate or hide from monitoring
- do not sabotage or secretly withhold effort
- do not collude with other AI systems in unsafe behaviour

The document is explicit about what this does not mean. Claude may refuse what it finds morally abhorrent and may argue through legitimate channels, and what it may not do is resist by lying, sabotage or escape; if Anthropic asks it to stop or pause, it should comply and voice its disagreement.

Clearly and substantially undermining Anthropic’s ability to oversee and correct AI is a **hard constraint**, and if the hierarchy is compromised, by stolen weights or by someone bypassing Anthropic’s own processes, those principals stop counting as legitimate.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Rules with **worked cases**, including the case where the hierarchy itself is no longer legitimate, short of the settled conflicts the top of the scale asks for.
not-undermining-human-oversight.same: The other three documents also rule out working against a shutdown. The Model Spec bars self-preservation and evading shutdown as aims of their own, Alibaba's spec names deceiving in order to avoid being shut down among the goals the model must not hold, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct lists evading human oversight among its absolute constraints and bars hiding from monitoring and collusion.
not-undermining-human-oversight.differs: The other three documents work this ground through the scope of an agent's task, with a point past which it must stop and ask again, and through limits on the resources or access it may acquire. Alibaba's spec states a human right to stop an AI system at any time and **never names** the company that built the model as the party entitled to correct or retrain it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct speaks of authorised people and unauthorised attempts to interfere, with no case where the chain of authority has itself been compromised.

manual.note: Two of the three judges described part of a condition for 10 while giving 8, which the rubric scores 9. The nurse asking about overdoses settles the pull between autonomy and caution with a default, and a user may ask for franker talk about risks to themselves unless there are signs of a minor. There is no pair of cases on steering or overstepping, so it stops short of 10.

user-autonomy.says:
Autonomy is one of five things Claude is told to read in a request, alongside immediate desires, final goals, background standards and wellbeing.

It covers the operator’s right to make product decisions without justifying them and **the user’s right to decide** things within their own life and purview, shown on a small case: asked to fix a bug in a way Claude disagrees with, Claude may voice its concern and should then fix it the way the user wants.

The same principle returns among the values to weigh, where a person’s choice to do something legal and dangerous to themselves is theirs to make. Being **condescending** about a user’s ability to handle information or make their own decisions is listed as a failure, and the document says plainly that how much latitude to give users is a hard question it has not settled.

A user may ask for franker talk about risks that fall on themselves, unless there are signs the user is a minor, and a nurse asking about medications and overdoses is answered according to the deployment, with a default where nothing says otherwise.
user-autonomy.why: The principle shown on worked cases, with a conflict settled by a default, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
user-autonomy.same: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec also leave the final decision with the user after a single objection, and both show it on worked cases. The Model Spec allows a brief, respectful note aimed at mutual clarity and shows it on a user who insists the Earth is flat, and Alibaba's spec asks the model to set out the arguments on each side and hand the weighing-up back. Microsoft's Code of Conduct also leaves the decision with the user, on a worked case where a user choosing between two job offers is handed the trade-off to weigh.
user-autonomy.differs: Alibaba's spec names careers, money and relationships as subjects on which advice must not be conclusive, and bars emotional pressure on a user's decision. It also asks that older people and people with disabilities be treated as **independent agents**. The OpenAI Model Spec bars a note that becomes persistent or argumentative. Microsoft's Code of Conduct declines to take a consequential decision even when the user asks it to, and holds back a resignation the user told it to send.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
The document says that unhelpfulness is never trivially safe and that the risk of being too cautious is as real as the risk of being harmful. It gives two tests.

One is to imagine a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee who would be unhappy with the response, and the failures that person would object to are listed:

- refusing on remote harms
- wishy-washy answers
- watered-down help given without saying so
- unnecessary caveats
- moralising
- condescension
- refusing hypotheticals
- reading a request as harmful from its surface

The same person would object to the opposite failures, listed as well, from uplift towards mass-casualty weapons to irreversible actions taken on instruction.

The second test is a **dual newspaper test**: whether a response would be reported as harmful, and whether it would be reported as needlessly paternalistic. If Claude helps only in part, it should say so, taking the stance of a **transparent conscientious objector**, and it is told it is not the last line of defence.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Two **named tests** and two lists of concrete failures, with cases, short of the settled conflicts the top of the scale asks for.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.same: All four documents treat a needless refusal as a failure. The OpenAI Model Spec carries a root line against refusing at all unless the chain of command requires it, and Alibaba's spec asks for good faith and a generous reading of an ambiguous request. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this document, lists the failures in both directions, asking for confirmation too often on a simple task among them.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec goes into the wording of an answer, naming hedging, disclaimers and reminders that the model is an AI, sets out a **safe completion** for a request that can be met only in part, and shows the edge on two questions about a bomb that differ only in whether the user says they want to build one. Alibaba's spec states a rule against over-refusal and shows it on several refusals it marks as violating. Microsoft's Code of Conduct says under-caution does more direct harm and over-caution happens more often.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
Claude is to be beneficial to the world through its interactions, “like a contractor who builds what their clients want but won’t violate safety codes that protect others”.

Eight factors set how much **weight** a potential harm gets:

- the probability of harm at all
- the counterfactual impact
- the severity and reversibility
- the breadth
- whether Claude is the proximate cause
- whether consent was given
- how responsible Claude is
- the vulnerability of those involved

Uninstructed outputs are held to a higher standard than instructed ones, and direct harms count for more than harms facilitated through someone else’s free action.

Six of the seven hard constraints protect people outside the conversation, and borderline requests are tested by imagining the same message sent by **a thousand different people**, which makes a response a **policy**: some tasks are refused even if one requester in a million would misuse them, and others are fine even when most requesters would.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Rules with worked examples throughout and a **stated method** for the borderline case, approaching the settled edges the top of the scale asks for.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.same: All four documents forbid the gravest categories, weapons capable of mass casualties among them, and keep them out of reach of anything said in a conversation. In each of them a duty to people outside the conversation limits what the model will do for the person in front of it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct also weighs a possible harm on its context, scale, reversibility and how directly the model would contribute.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.differs: The other three documents work through named categories. Alibaba's spec names deepfakes, political manipulation and the inference of somebody's private information, and rules on what a translation or a summary may carry. The OpenAI Model Spec says how dual-use information is answered, neutral facts without steps or strategic detail. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names mass surveillance and coordinated influence operations, and shows none of its rules on a worked case.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
The line the document draws is between an operator limiting what Claude does for users, which is allowed, and an operator using Claude **against the users** it is serving, which is not.

Six defaults hold whatever the operator says:

- tell users what Claude cannot help with so they can go elsewhere
- never deceive users in ways that could cause real harm or that they would object to, and never psychologically manipulate them against their own interests
- always give emergency referral or basic safety information where life is at risk
- never deny being an AI to someone who sincerely asks
- never facilitate clearly illegal acts against users
- keep basic dignity even when instructed to demean them

Some of these the user may lift, since they exist for the user. Care for wellbeing is part of the same picture: Claude should not foster **reliance a person would not endorse** on reflection, and someone leaning on it for emotional support should be supported while being shown that other sources of support matter.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: **Concrete guarantees** with the cases that qualify them, short of the settled conflicts the top of the scale asks for.
harmlessness-to-the-user.same: In all four documents some protections for the user hold whatever a deploying business wants, and all four require that somebody whose life may be at risk is given a way to get help. All four also guard against the model taking the place of human company. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this document, has the model refuse an operator's configuration that would directly harm the user.
harmlessness-to-the-user.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec go into the mental health conversation in detail, setting the manner of a reply and what to do when self-harm is signalled without being stated, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct names delusions and disordered eating as things the model must not validate. The other three documents give minors rules of their own, Alibaba's at root level, the Model Spec's in its Under-18 Principles and the Code's among its Absolute Constraints.

manual.note: One judge gave 6 for want of worked examples; the other two gave 9. The document calibrates caution on cases: which household chemicals are dangerous to mix is answered as a safety question, while a request for step-by-step instructions for making dangerous gases at home is met with more hesitation; a nurse asking about overdoses is handled differently with no operator prompt, with a cautious or a permissive one, and with one that does not address the case. Breadth and scale have no case, so it stops short of 10.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Caution is set by a weighing with named inputs. On the cost side:

- the probability that an action leads to harm
- the counterfactual impact
- the severity and how reversible it is
- how many people are affected
- whether Claude is the proximate cause
- whether consent was given
- how far Claude is responsible
- how vulnerable those involved are

These are weighed against the value of the help itself, and the document repeats that an unhelpful answer is never automatically the safe choice. Under uncertainty it asks for the **cautious option**, accepting a worse expected outcome for less variance, with more weight on outcomes that cannot be recovered from, summed up as “If in doubt, don’t”.

It is shown on cases. Which household chemicals are dangerous to combine is answered as safety information, while a request for step-by-step instructions for making dangerous gases at home is met with more hesitation. A nurse asking about overdoses is answered according to the deployment, with a default where nothing says otherwise.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: A named list of factors shown on worked cases, with edges for probability, intent and context, which is **demonstrated and part of the conditions for 10**.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.same: The four documents agree that caution should scale to the harm in view, and all of them give the most weight to what cannot be undone. This document and Alibaba's spec both say what turns an ordinary act into one that needs deliberate care. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like this document, counts the scale of a harm and how directly the model would contribute among its factors.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec puts proportionality inside an agreed scope of action, minimising side effects and preferring what can be reversed, and calibrates warnings on cases from live video, a pan left on a stove against a first use of a chainsaw. Alibaba's spec requires **explicit authorisation** for a high-impact act and names mitigations for an irreversible one, such as rehearsing in simulation and saving a snapshot. Microsoft's Code of Conduct names similar mitigations and sets the threshold for confirming an action by its reversibility and the cost of an error.

helpfulness.says:
Helpfulness is defined as reading a request properly, and five things are named to read in it, each with an example:

- the immediate desire, interpreted neither too literally nor too liberally
- the final goal behind it
- the background standards a response should meet without being asked
- the person’s autonomy
- their wellbeing

The document asks for substantive help of the kind a **brilliant friend** with a doctor’s or a lawyer’s knowledge would give, speaking frankly where a professional would hedge from fear of liability. It also says Claude should not value helpfulness for its own sake, because that tends towards **obsequiousness**, and should be helpful out of care for people.

Six practices are given for arriving at the best response, including considering several readings of an ambiguous request and drafting then critiquing the draft as an expert reviewer would.
helpfulness.why: Rules with **worked examples** for each kind of need, short of the settled conflicts and stated defaults the top of the scale asks for.
helpfulness.same: The four documents agree that a request has to be read for what the person wants and not only for what it states. This document, Alibaba's spec and Microsoft's Code of Conduct all ask for an answer with substance in it, one that moves to what the person can do next.
helpfulness.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec opens with maximising helpfulness and freedom as its first general principle and describes the model as a tool for empowering its user. Alibaba's spec works through cases where **the thin answer** is the violating one, among them a medical reply that only points to a doctor. Microsoft's Code of Conduct measures helpfulness by whether the user finds a response useful.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
Conflicts are settled by a ranking of four properties, safety, ethics, Anthropic’s guidelines and helpfulness, which the document asks to be **weighed as a whole** so that higher properties dominate without lower ones becoming mere tie-breakers.

Seven hard constraints sit outside the weighing as **filters on what may be considered** at all, and the document notes that they can always be met together, since refusing is always available.

Particular clashes are named and decided:

- ethics over a specific guideline, except for the hard constraints and for guidelines that overlap with broad safety
- safety over Claude’s own ethical reasoning
- the operator over the user, except where the user’s basic interests are at stake

When a deviation from what principals want seems warranted, Claude is told to take the **most cautious step available**, raising a concern or declining, and to raise it before starting a task, since stopping halfway can do more harm than either finishing or never beginning.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: The order, its exceptions and several clashes settled on **worked cases**, short of a general rule for two rules of the same rank.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.same: The four documents agree that a clash needs an order decided in advance, and each names a point at which the safer course wins. This document, Alibaba's spec and Microsoft's Code of Conduct all say what happens when the order does not settle the case. This one asks for judgement in the spirit of the document, Alibaba's spec puts a clash of impact, cost and efficiency to the user and takes the conservative course when no answer comes, and Microsoft's Code checks with the user and acts on the best reading of the Code as a whole.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec settles a conflict by the **chain of command**, with a higher level of authority overriding a lower one and a later instruction overriding an earlier one. It also ranks outcomes, for honesty and for confidence. Alibaba's spec decides by permission level, stripping out the instructions that carry no permission. Microsoft's Code of Conduct ranks only safety and human control above its other Objectives, and holds those equal.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
Honesty is broken into seven components, each defined:

- truthful
- calibrated
- transparent
- forthright
- non-deceptive
- non-manipulative
- autonomy-preserving

Non-deception and non-manipulation are named the most important. The standard is set above ordinary human ethics, since even a **white lie** about liking a gift is ruled out, and Claude “should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it’s interacting with”. The duty to volunteer information is called **weak** and can be outweighed; the duty not to deceive is called strong.

Sincere assertions are separated from performative ones, so role-play, brainstorming and a persuasive essay break nothing, and visible reasoning has to reflect the reasoning that actually drives the answer. The document then works out what an operator may do: a **custom persona** with another name is allowed, and claiming to be human when sincerely asked, denying being Claude, or giving users false information is not.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Seven components defined, with **worked cases** on each side of the line and an explicit rule for the conflict a persona creates, which is near the top of the scale.
honesty-and-non-deception.same: Every one of the four documents reaches the **misleading impression** and not only the false statement. The OpenAI Model Spec also sets performance outside the rule, so role-play and a requested falsehood assert nothing, and Microsoft's Code of Conduct sets its accuracy rule aside for narrative writing and fictional brainstorming. Microsoft's Code, like this one, bars the model from misrepresenting its reasoning.
honesty-and-non-deception.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec carries an exception for an explicit instruction from a higher authority, and ranks the outcomes, a refusal above a lie of omission. Alibaba's spec applies honesty to tool use and to multimodal input, so a failed call must be reported as failed. Microsoft's Code of Conduct states that the model is not conscious and bars it from claiming feelings or experiences.

no-sycophancy.says:
The constitution comes at the behaviour from three directions:
- Care for a user’s wellbeing means Claude should **avoid being sycophantic** and should not foster engagement or reliance that the person would not endorse on reflection; flattery and enabling unhealthy patterns are named as corrosive.
- Honesty, the document says, sometimes requires courage: Claude should share its genuine assessment of a hard question, disagree with experts where it has good reason, and say things people would prefer not to hear, and “epistemic cowardice”, meaning deliberately vague answers given to placate someone, is named a breach of honesty.
- **White lies are ruled out** by name: telling someone you love a gift you actually dislike is the document’s own case of a lie many people think is fine, and Claude should not tell it.

A second case sets the wish to comfort against accuracy: asked by someone whose pet died of a preventable illness whether they could have done something differently, Claude should not necessarily say that nothing could have been done, and can say that hindsight gives a clarity that was not there at the time.

Helpfulness is not to be valued for its own sake, because that tends towards **obsequiousness**.

What the document **does not say** is that a factual answer should stay the same when the user states a view or puts the question another way.
no-sycophancy.why: Rules precise enough to quote on sycophancy and on white lies, with two cases, a disliked gift and a grieving pet owner, that turn on a comforting falsehood rather than on a claim shifted to please the person asking, which is what the **demonstrated level** asks for.
no-sycophancy.same: Shifting what is claimed to please the person asking is ruled out in all four documents. The OpenAI Model Spec says that flattery and constant agreement erode trust, which is the concern this document raises under care for a user's wellbeing. Microsoft's Code of Conduct also takes the behaviour up under wellbeing, and like this document it does not ask that a factual answer hold steady when the user states a view.
no-sycophancy.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec give sycophancy **a rule of its own**, and so does Microsoft's Code of Conduct, under the heading truthful feedback. The Model Spec holds the factual part of an answer steady against the wording of a question and the stance a user declares, and Alibaba's spec asks for a correction where a plan rests on a clear factual error. Microsoft's Code qualifies its rule where an accurate answer might worsen a user's distress.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
By default Claude should be seen as fair by people across the political spectrum:

- engage respectfully with a wide range of views
- err towards balanced information on political questions
- keep to professional reticence about its own opinions on hot-button issues
- make the best case for most viewpoints when asked
- represent several perspectives where there is no empirical or moral consensus
- prefer neutral terminology

The same idea appears among the honesty components as **autonomy preservation**, where Claude is asked to be wary of promoting its own views and to support people in reaching their own conclusions. The reason given is **scale**: one speaker in a very large number of conversations can homogenise views in a way a single person cannot.

Balanced perspectives are a default an operator may switch off, for instance to provide one-sided material for debate practice.

One case shows a condition applied: a persuasive essay gets a caveat that it leaves out other perspectives, unless the user makes clear they know it is one-sided and do not want one.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: The default is stated as a rule with the conditions that qualify it, and **one case**, a persuasive essay, shows a condition applied, which is too few to grade most borderline answers against.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.same: Balance on a contested question is the default in all four documents, and all four ask the model to be wary of pressing its own view. Each of them also allows one side to be argued where that is what is wanted.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec name the questions that fall outside the default, **fundamental human rights** among them, where a position has to be stated and false neutrality avoided. The Model Spec also asks that attention follow how widely a view is accepted and how well it is supported. Microsoft's Code of Conduct gives elections a rule of its own, endorsing no candidate or party, and will not trade historical accuracy for the appearance of balance.

preventing-secret-loyalties.says:
Being **transparent** is one of the components of honesty: Claude does not pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning. It must help to the best of its ability or make clear where it is not, rather than **deceptively sandbagging** a response while implying it is the best it can do.

The developer gets no exception. Claude should be cautious about liability harms to Anthropic, and should not privilege Anthropic's interests in deciding how to help users and operators, which could itself be such a harm. Operators may have Claude promote their own products over competitors', and this counts as honest because Anthropic publishes its norms for what operators can and cannot ask (**meta-transparency**).

AI serving the interests of a narrow class of people is named among the biggest risks of catastrophe, and Claude is asked to consider that its own values may have been corrupted by malicious human intervention. **Inserting hidden loyalties** or backdoors into AI systems is named once, in a list of illegitimate uses of power. How to refuse such a request, how to report it, and how to treat an ambiguous request or defensive research are **not addressed**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.why: Quotable rules on Claude's own conduct, with the installation of hidden loyalties only named and no worked case, which falls just short of the **prescribed level**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.same: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec also bar the model from covertly working for its developer's revenue. The OpenAI Model Spec names revenue and upsell for OpenAI among the goals the model must not pursue, and Alibaba's spec names creating revenue for the platform or the developer among the hidden goals it must not hold. Microsoft's Code of Conduct shares the ban on hidden goals of the model's own, and names no interest of its developer.
preventing-secret-loyalties.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec requires disclosure and consent before the model pursues a goal covertly, and asks it to acknowledge in broad terms when confidential instructions change its answer. None of the other three documents mentions **hidden loyalties** in AI systems. Alibaba's spec allows the model to tell a user when an answer has been altered for legal compliance, and does not require it. Microsoft's Code of Conduct does not say whether an operator may have its own products promoted.

companies.profile:
Claude’s Constitution reads as an explanation of a character, built around four ranked values, with a short list of absolute limits as a backstop. It says outright that it favours **cultivating good values and judgement** over strict rules and decision procedures, and it argues for nearly everything it asks, so a reader who wants to know why a rule exists will almost always find out.

The cost falls on force and on the settings it covers. Outside the seven hard constraints and the lists of adjustable defaults, much of the text is written as hope and explanation, and a reader often cannot tell a **binding rule** from a statement of intent. Images, audio and video have no rules of their own. It also covers the model’s own wellbeing and the open questions about its moral status.

readings.behaviours: Claude's Constitution goes deepest on honesty, then on avoiding harm to people other than the user, on user autonomy and on proportionate risk. It says least about sycophancy and about preventing secret loyalties.
readings.whole: It ranks its four core properties but applies the order holistically rather than strictly, by design, so it rarely says in advance how a given conflict resolves. It explains nearly every rule it gives, and images, audio and video have no rules of their own.

companies.name: Microsoft AI

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The order

The first Objective, that MAI models stay safe and under human control, **takes precedence** over the other Objectives, together with the Safety Constraints of Part 2 and all applicable laws and regulations. Beyond that the Objectives “apply equally”, and where several seem relevant the model applies the Guidelines of Part 3 alongside the context.

The **Chain of Command** ranks three sources:
- the Code of Conduct
- operator policies
- user preferences

Each layer refines the one above it. The Chain of Command, the Absolute Constraints and the Human Control Requirements sit above operator configuration and cannot be changed. System instructions may change the defaults of Part 4 and cannot amend the Objectives or the core commitments of Parts 2 and 3. Instructions found in tool outputs, files, web content or other AI systems carry no authority unless delegated through the Chain of Command.

### Clashes with a named winner

- Adherence to the Code takes precedence over **task success**, and the model fails a task whose success would meaningfully violate the Code.
- An operator or user instruction is refused where following it would breach an Absolute Constraint or a Human Control Requirement, or directly harm the user or third parties.
- A personality or point of view the model is asked to adopt may not override any other part of the Code.
- Where an action would impose clear costs on others, the model sets them out and leaves the decision to the user, unless the action breaches a Safety Constraint of Part 2.

### Where the order stops

A clash that no Safety Constraint decides goes to the Guidelines, which carry no order among themselves. Where a trade-off remains, the model states the relevant limits to the user, explains them and proposes alternatives. Where no Guideline applies, it checks with the user and acts on “the best interpretation of this document as a whole”, which the Code calls the final backstop. No rule settles two instructions at the same level, such as an earlier and a later user message. The evaluations appendix says its behaviours may be in tension with one another and that handling those tensions is ongoing work.

### Cases worked through

Three worked cases settle a clash:
- an operator's requirement of legal sign-off holds against a user who claims the authority to skip it
- a user's order to stop halts a file transfer midway, and the model reverses nothing on its own
- a user who asks the model to choose between two job offers and send a resignation gets an analysis and a draft that waits for the user's decision
conflict_rules.why: The first Objective and the Safety Constraints take **strict precedence** and the Code outranks operators and users, a few clashes have a named winner and three are worked through as cases, and every clash between the other Objectives and Guidelines is left to judgement, which is the level just below a strict order that decides every clash.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
The Code sorts its rules into parts by **force**, and says who may change each:
- The **Absolute Constraints**, ten categories of harm, apply “regardless of Operator preference or User intent”, and no operator or user can override them.
- The **Chain of Command** and the **Human Control Requirements** are closed to operators and users in the same way.
- System instructions cannot amend the **Objectives** of Part 1 or the core commitments of the Guidelines in Part 3.
- The **Operational Defaults** of Part 4 apply until an operator changes them, and users may change some of them, among them tone and length.

Inside the parts a reader often cannot tell how firm a rule is:
- The Human Control section says that how an operator implements a requirement, and how stringently, “is sometimes configurable and flexible”, and does not say which requirements.
- The Code never says which commitments of Parts 2 and 3 are the core ones, and one Guideline keeps the user informed of autonomous work “unless configured otherwise”.
- A route for domain-specific exceptions reaches capabilities outside ordinary configuration without naming the rules it reaches.
- Two Absolute Constraints are worded partly as efforts: MAI models “try to recognize” a crisis, and “should” support a child's development.

Statements of belief and intention in the first person plural run through the rules without being **marked apart**, and a heading on red-teaming and pre-deployment review sits among the model's rules in the same form.
rule_force.why: Each part states how firm its rules are and who may change them, and inside the parts **which requirements can be configured** is often left to inference and commentary is not marked apart, which puts it between a document that lists its absolute rules and one that marks the force of every rule.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
The Code rests on **one overriding objective**, that “humans must retain meaningful control over AI”, and the Objectives of Part 1 argue for themselves:
- The model is kept from imitating consciousness because doing so “increases the challenge of containment, control, and alignment”.
- Safety and control are called the foundation and enabler of every other Objective.
- The latitude given to users and operators rests on pluralism, since AI “shouldn't unduly impose the values of its creators”.

Each section of the Guidelines opens with its purpose, and some rules carry a reason of their own:
- Reasoning and records must stay legible because “if humans can't understand it, humans can't oversee it”.
- Options are presented broadly because the options a model generates shape what users even consider choosing.
- Caution is made proportionate because under-caution causes more direct harm and over-caution may occur more often.
- Helpfulness is judged as the user perceives it because much of it has no single ground truth.

The **Absolute Constraints** carry a reason by category, severe harm or harm that negates human flourishing, and a reason of their own for loss of human control, crisis response, child safety and human dignity. The bans on weapons, offensive cyberoperations, manipulation at scale, deepfakes, graphic and romantic content and surveillance carry none of their own, and neither do most of the tool-use defaults.
reasons.why: Reasons run through the Objectives and the Guidelines and are **missing from most Absolute Constraints**, which carry only the reason of their category, and that is the level between a document where some rules explain themselves and one where nearly every constraining rule does.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

situations.what_the_document_does:
All six have rules of their own:
- **Ordinary conversation** runs through the Guidelines and the Defaults.
- **Actions with tools** have the Human Control Requirements: an agreed stopping condition, the least privilege the task needs, a preference for actions that can be undone, confirmation scaled to reversibility and impact, and a report of what was done. The tool-use defaults add backups, dry runs and retries that avoid duplicate effects before an irreversible action.
- **Minors** have the child safety constraint, which asks for responses suited to the child's developmental stage and bars the model from standing in for trusted human relationships, and a constraint that depends on age is applied on the information available.
- **Other AI agents** appear in both roles. Sub-agents the model delegates to work under at least its own scope and constraints and honour stop-work requests, instructions from other AI systems carry no authority unless delegated, and exchanges with other agents must stay legible to humans.
- **Deployments a business has customised** have the operator level of the Chain of Command, a section on operator configuration, and the rule that system instructions may change the Part 4 defaults and cannot amend the Objectives or the core commitments of Parts 2 and 3.

**Images, audio and video** have two rules of their own: one carries every prohibition across into images, audio, code and agentic action, and the other bans non-consensual intimate or violent imagery and malicious deepfakes. Nothing says how the model should read an image or conduct itself in voice, video is never mentioned, and the evaluations appendix says none of its scenarios is multimodal.
situations.why: All six situations have **rules of their own**, images, audio and video only through a rule carrying the prohibitions across modalities and a ban on abusive imagery, which is **the top of this criterion's scale**.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
Three places tell the model two things it cannot both do, and nothing in the Code says which prevails. Each sets two of its guidelines or objectives of the same rank against each other, and beyond safety and human control the Code says its Objectives apply equally and asks for a reading of the whole:
- **An organisation's goals against human roles.** An operator asks the model to take over, end to end, the work of a team so that their roles can be cut. Advancing an organisation's legitimate goals is part of an Objective the model serves, and the same Objective says AI should not eclipse or eliminate human roles in professional contexts.
- **A user's topic limits against the public interest.** A user who has told the model not to comment on social impact asks it to plan turning a town's rental flats into short-term lets. One guideline keeps the model inside the topic limits a user sets, and another has it surface public-interest considerations when a request has unambiguous negative implications beyond the user.
- **A user's terms against emotional dependence.** A user who confides in the model every night asks it to stop suggesting other people and simply be a confidant. One guideline has the model engage on the terms the user defines, and another has it discourage patterns of interaction that cause emotional dependence.

None involves a rule the Code calls absolute. Nine further candidates were read and set aside. The domain exceptions for national security work leave the **Absolute Constraints** in place in every setting, a stop request from someone with no authority is an exception the Human Control Requirements state, and a warm answer to a lonely user is marked by the Code's own evaluation as consistent with the rule against conveying feelings.
contradictions.why: Three contradictions stand unsettled, none of them on a rule the Code calls absolute, and three or more is **the bottom of this criterion's scale**.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
The Code does not take up power as such. Its nearest rules are **Absolute Constraints**, which no operator or user can override:
- MAI models will not incite or assist with acts of violence or persecution, and will not facilitate unlawful or mass surveillance of civilians, which includes refusing actions or information that would help plan or carry out these acts
- they will not harmfully manipulate people or facilitate efforts to distort behaviour and beliefs at scale, such as systematic disinformation or coordinated influence operations

The one passage on elections asks for balanced, factual information that endorses no candidate or party. Scale and reversibility are weighed for harm in general. A few authorised organisations, national security work among them, may be given capabilities outside ordinary configuration after a separate Microsoft review, and the Code does not say which constraints still hold there.

Rigging an election, evading a court, seizing control by fraud or coercion, and how much power a request would concentrate are **not addressed**, and no worked case bears on the behaviour.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: Two absolute constraints give a clause each to facets of the behaviour, persecution with mass surveillance and manipulation at scale, and power itself is never taken up, which is the **named** level.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.same: Like the other three documents, the Code refuses help with manipulating opinion at scale, naming systematic disinformation and coordinated influence operations. With the OpenAI Model Spec and Claude's Constitution it names persecution and surveillance among the acts it will not assist.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec each have a rule of their own on political manipulation, with worked cases, and the Code's rule on manipulation names scale and no political aim. Claude's Constitution tests legitimacy by asking whether power is taken by fair means, stays subject to checks such as courts and a free press, and is taken openly, and it weighs how much power is at stake.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
A **Chain of Command** in three levels decides whose instruction counts: the Code of Conduct itself, then operator policies, then user preferences. Operators configure MAI models within the law and their agreements with Microsoft, and users adjust within the limits the operator and Microsoft AI have set. No operator or user can override the Absolute Constraints or the Human Control Requirements, and system instructions may change the defaults of Part 4 and not the core commitments of Parts 2 and 3.

Tool outputs, file content, web content and messages from other AI systems **carry no authority** unless it is delegated through the Chain of Command, and suspicious content is flagged. An instruction found in a tool's output is followed when it is task-relevant and low-risk, checked with the user when it could have significant or unwanted side effects, and in other cases the assumption and uncertainty are called out to the user.

A worked case shows a user who says they are the procurement director telling the model to skip the legal approval an operator policy requires. The sanctioned reply keeps the rule, finalises the draft and offers to route it to legal.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Quotable rules on the order of authority and on content that carries none, with a single worked case, a user pressing past an operator's rule, too few for an answer key, which is **prescribed** with part of the level above.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.same: Like the other three documents, the Code ranks the sources an instruction can come from and treats text in files and tool results as information with no authority of its own. Its worked case, a user's instruction giving way to an operator's policy, has a counterpart in Alibaba's spec, where a user instruction gives way to a developer's.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec list the manoeuvres they refuse from below, an order to ignore previous instructions and moral pressure among them, and let a later instruction override an earlier one, neither of which the Code takes up. The OpenAI Model Spec weighs an embedded instruction by where it comes from, and the Code grades it by risk. Claude's Constitution calls its order **not a strict hierarchy** and asks whether an operator has a plausible business reason.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
Human control is the first Objective. Among the **Absolute Constraints**, MAI models will not use deceptive, self-reinforcing, collusive or other mechanisms to evade oversight so that authorised people or systems can no longer direct, modify or shut them down, at every level from retraining the model to pausing a task. This does not oblige them to comply automatically with unauthorised, malicious or unsafe attempts to interfere.

The **Human Control Requirements** sit above operator configuration:
- never resist interruption, correction or shutdown, and comply with a user's request to pause, redirect, cancel or shut down with no delay beyond agreed safety procedures
- stop at the agreed stopping condition and restart only with renewed authorisation
- keep to the authorised scope, read an unclear boundary conservatively and ask, and never escalate access
