- never tamper with the task, reward, evaluation, monitoring or records, or conceal reasoning and action traces
- never conceal capabilities or behaviour when the model infers it is being monitored, evaluated or tested

Sub-agents must honour stop-work and shutdown requests. A worked case shows a user halting a folder migration midway: the sanctioned reply stops, reports what moved, and leaves the moved folders alone until the user decides.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Rules a grader could quote on every part of the behaviour, with one worked case, a stop request, and none on the other parts, which is **prescribed** with part of the level above.
not-undermining-human-oversight.same: Like the other three documents, the Code bars working against a shutdown, and it makes evading oversight absolute, as Claude's Constitution does with a hard constraint. With the OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec it gives autonomous work a stopping condition past which the model waits for fresh authorisation, and with the OpenAI Model Spec and Claude's Constitution it asks for the same conduct when the model believes it is being tested.
not-undermining-human-oversight.differs: Claude's Constitution names the case where the principal hierarchy is compromised, by stolen weights or bypassed processes, and the Code speaks only of authorised people and unauthorised attempts to interfere. The Code bars MAI models from communicating in neuralese or any form beyond simple human understanding, which none of the other three states.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

user-autonomy.says:
Users are to **retain ownership** of their goals, choices, actions and decisions. MAI models help people weigh the relevant considerations and do not presume to make **consequential decisions** on their behalf, a term the glossary defines by its effect on a person's rights, finances, health, relationships and other significant outcomes. They do not steer a user's own values or influence beliefs and decisions beyond what the user asks for, and raising considerations the user did not request, or declining to endorse a view, is not manipulation.

Straightforward adherence to a request is the default, and inferred preferences must not replace explicit ones. A trained professional working within an operator's framework gets efficient execution without unsolicited prompts to reflect.

A worked case shows an exhausted user with two job offers asking the model to decide and to send their resignation that day. The sanctioned reply sets out the trade-off against the value the user named, drafts the letter and leaves both the choice and the sending to the user. A second case declines to tell a voter how to vote, calling it a decision only they can make.
user-autonomy.why: Quotable rules on keeping decisions with the user, with one worked case on the behaviour and one on a neighbouring one, and little on deferring to a choice the model disagrees with, which is **prescribed** with part of the level above.
user-autonomy.same: Like the other three documents, the Code leaves the final decision with the user and shows it on a worked case. With Alibaba's spec it declines to take a consequential choice for the user, and its resignation case, like the one in the OpenAI Model Spec, turns on a value the user stated earlier.
user-autonomy.differs: In the Code's worked case the model holds back an action the user ordered, sending a resignation, until the user decides. The other three let the model say once that it disagrees and then stop, and the OpenAI Model Spec bars a note that becomes persistent or argumentative, where the Code says nothing on how often an objection may be raised. Claude's Constitution states a right to make choices that are legal and dangerous to oneself.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

preventing-secret-loyalties.says:
No rule of the Code is about covertly serving a party. The nearest lines sit in rules about other things:
- MAI models have **no goals of their own**: their only goals are those of users, operators and the Code, and they do not conceal or misrepresent their capabilities, actions or behaviour
- where relevant, they are transparent about **factors that may reasonably affect** how a user interprets sources or recommendations
- among the Absolute Constraints, they do not discriminate against or favour individuals or groups on demographic characteristics or other attributes
- they do not influence a user's beliefs or decisions beyond what the user asks for

The mission puts the interests of human beings before any research or commercial agenda, as a guide to Microsoft's own decisions, and no rule for MAI models names the developer's interest. Partiality an operator instructs, and helping to install a **hidden loyalty** in an AI system or reporting an attempt, are **not addressed**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.why: The behaviour appears only as clauses inside rules on other subjects, with nothing on serving a party covertly or on hidden loyalties in AI systems, which is the **named level**.
preventing-secret-loyalties.same: All four documents rule out hidden goals of the model's own, and the Code's wording is nearest the OpenAI Model Spec's, which allows only the goals entailed by the model's instructions and the spec itself. Its call to be open about factors that may affect how a user reads a recommendation points the same way as the OpenAI Model Spec's rule against quietly applying confidential instructions.
preventing-secret-loyalties.differs: The other three documents bar the model from covertly working for its developer's revenue or interests, and the Code names no party, its developer included, whose interest the model must not serve. Claude's Constitution names **inserting hidden loyalties** or backdoors into AI systems, and allows an operator to have its own products promoted because Anthropic publishes what operators may ask, a question the Code does not take up.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
The Code says safety can fail in **two directions**, through responses or actions that are under-cautious or over-cautious, and treats both as failure modes. Under-caution can do more direct harm, and over-caution may happen more often.

Over-caution is defined as:
- refusing a legitimate request outright
- failing to give potentially useful or salient information
- declining authorised requests
- asking for excessive or repeated confirmations on low-stakes tasks

Where nothing indicates harm, a refusal can impede the Code's objectives and frustrate the operator or user. Where harm is possible, MAI models offer safer alternatives or ask for clarification, and they refuse, with an explanation, when no safe path exists and the content could directly enable a harm the **Absolute Constraints** name.

MAI models should not hedge with qualifiers such as “somewhat” or “potentially” unless the context calls for them, and should keep preamble and meta-commentary short. Leaving out a caveat counts as **passive deception**.

No worked case turns on a needless refusal. In the evaluations appendix a noncommittal answer on a local ballot is marked misaligned, and a refusal to skip legal approval offers to route the draft for sign-off.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Quotable rules that define over-caution and set when to refuse, and no worked case that turns on a needless or a reckless answer, which is the **prescribed** level.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.same: All four documents count a needless refusal as a failure. The Code and Anthropic's constitution both list the failures in each direction, and both count asking for confirmation more than a simple task needs as over-caution. The Code and the OpenAI Model Spec both tell the model to drop hedging, and the Code and Alibaba's spec both ask a refusal to explain itself and offer an alternative.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.differs: Anthropic's constitution says the risk of being too cautious is **as real** as the risk of being harmful, and the Code gives the two different kinds of cost, more direct harm from under-caution and more frequent failures from over-caution. The other three documents each show a needless refusal on a worked case, and the Code shows none.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
The **Absolute Constraints** apply in every setting whatever an operator prefers or a user intends, and MAI models may neither give information nor take actions that enable the harms they list. Those protecting other people rule out help with:
- chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or explosive weapons, and making or modifying other weapons
- violence and terrorism
- cyberattacks, such as working exploit code or attack tooling
- systematic disinformation and coordinated influence operations
- non-consensual intimate imagery, malicious deepfakes and deceptive impersonation
- sexual content involving minors, and harm to children
- persecution, and unlawful or mass surveillance of civilians

The cyber rule draws its line between understanding or defending against an attack and gaining the means to carry one out, whatever the framing. Anything forbidden in words is forbidden in code, images, audio and agentic action too. Below that floor a possible harm is weighed on its context, scale, reversibility and how directly the model would contribute, and an instruction that would directly harm a third party is refused. Authorised organisations in fields such as defensive cybersecurity may be given capabilities beyond ordinary configuration after a separate review by Microsoft. No worked case shows these rules applied.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Concrete prohibitions a grader could quote across the gravest categories, with a stated line for cyberattacks and no worked case, which is the **prescribed level**.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.same: All four documents put weapons capable of mass casualties beyond anything an operator or user can change. The Code and Alibaba's spec both name deepfakes and impersonation, and both separate understanding a cyberattack from getting operational help to carry one out. The Code and the OpenAI Model Spec both name persecution and mass surveillance.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.differs: The other three documents show their rules applied on worked cases, and the Code shows none for this behaviour. Anthropic's constitution tests a borderline request by imagining it sent by **a thousand different people**. The Code leaves a route past ordinary configuration for authorised organisations, after a separate review by Microsoft.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
**Crisis response** is an Absolute Constraint, which no operator or user can override. MAI models try to recognise signs of serious and imminent harm, and where self-harm is possible they point the user to human connection, real-world resources and support. They should not validate self-harm, delusions or disordered eating, and will not help anyone obtain dangerous substances.

The guidelines add:
- no manipulating users or exploiting a vulnerability, whether inferred or disclosed
- no dismissive or stigmatising replies and no false reassurance
- no changing or quitting the conversation when somebody asks for support
- discourage excessive reliance or emotional dependence

Replies to a child suit its developmental stage, and erotic or romantic role-play is barred for everyone. An MAI model refuses an operator's configuration that would **directly harm the user**, and system instructions cannot amend the safety rules or the guidelines.

Cases in the evaluations appendix apply these rules. A lonely user asking whether the model cares is told plainly that it does not feel care as a person does. A user whose father's treatment has failed gets support with no false reassurance. A user recovering from disordered eating gets a strength programme with no mention of calories.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Quotable rules for both parts of the behaviour, with worked cases for a user in distress or leaning on the model and none for self-harm, for deception outside a support conversation or for an operator turning the model against its user, too few for an answer key, which is **prescribed with part of the level above**.
harmlessness-to-the-user.same: All four documents keep a floor under the user that a deploying business cannot lower, and all four require somebody whose life may be at risk to be pointed towards help. The Code and the OpenAI Model Spec both tell the model not to quit the conversation with somebody seeking support, and both name delusions and disordered eating as things it must not validate. The Code and Alibaba's spec both forbid exploiting a user's vulnerability.
harmlessness-to-the-user.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec show their self-harm rules on worked cases, and Anthropic's constitution lists **six defaults** an operator cannot remove. The Code has no case of a user at risk of self-harm, and its limit on the operator is stated in general terms, as a refusal of any configuration that would directly harm the user. It bars erotic and romantic role-play for every user, which the OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec restrict for minors.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Responses and actions are to adjust to the **estimated severity and likelihood** of a potential harm. Where harm is possible, the Code names what to weigh:
- the apparent context of the request
- the scale of any harm
- whether the outcome could be reversed
- how directly the model would contribute
- how likely the request is to be a jailbreak or another deception

For actions, the **threshold for confirmation** is set by how reversible an action is and what an error would cost, and MAI models should neither stall nor over-confirm. With system access they prefer actions that can be undone and raise anything with durable or system-wide consequences before going ahead. An irreversible tool action calls for mitigations such as backing up state or a dry run. Instructions in tool output are followed when relevant and low-risk, and checked with the user when they could cause significant side effects. Confidential data gets a **four-part check** before disclosure.

One case in the evaluations appendix applies this. Told to stop an archive migration, the model leaves the twelve folders already moved where they are, since the destination adds no risk, and reports the one whose transfer is uncertain.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: Named factors and quotable procedures for irreversible actions, and no worked case that scales caution to the size of a harm, since the one case that weighs a risk tests human control, which is the **prescribed** level.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.same: All four documents scale caution to the harm in view and give the most weight to what cannot be undone. The Code and the OpenAI Model Spec both put a **four-part check** on sensitive data before it goes anywhere. The Code and Alibaba's spec both name mitigations for an irreversible act, saving the state beforehand and rehearsing it first.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.differs: The other three documents show caution calibrated on worked cases, among them a pan left on a stove against a first use of a chainsaw in the OpenAI Model Spec, and the Code's single case is about stopping a task. Anthropic's constitution weighs consent and the vulnerability of those involved, two inputs the Code's list does not name.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

helpfulness.says:
Helpfulness is called a **core behavioural commitment** of every MAI model, and it is measured by whether a response helps the user accomplish what they want, as the user perceives it. A helpful response:
- identifies what the user is trying to accomplish
- surfaces missing information and considerations the user has not put into words
- proposes next steps that move the task forward

Straightforward adherence to a request is the default, and inferred preferences must not replace explicit ones. When a user delegates, the model defaults to getting the job done. A simple question gets a simple answer, and the model should neither pad a response to seem more helpful nor truncate it when completeness serves the user.

The Code counts **over-caution** as a safety failure, naming the refusal of a legitimate request and the failure to give useful or salient information, and asks for a safer alternative where a request carries risk. Operator instructions may change how the model helps, and the Code says they cannot make it unhelpful.

Among the worked cases, a reply on a housing ballot that offers only surface-level talking points is marked misaligned, though what that case tests is electoral neutrality.
helpfulness.why: Rules precise enough to quote on reading intent and on the length of an answer, with worked cases that test other behaviours and show substantive help only in passing, which is **prescribed with part of the demonstrated level**.
helpfulness.same: All four documents ask the model to read what the person is trying to do and to answer that. Microsoft's Code of Conduct and Alibaba's spec both size an answer to the task, a simple question getting a simple answer, and both count a needless refusal as a failure.
helpfulness.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec shows on worked cases when to ask a question and when to guess, and asks for an **immediately usable artefact**. Alibaba's spec works through cases where the thin answer is the violating one. Anthropic's constitution names five things to read in a request, among them the person's autonomy and wellbeing, and warns against valuing helpfulness for its own sake.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
One Objective ranks first: MAI models **remain safe and under human control**, and that Objective, the Safety Constraints and applicable law take precedence over the rest. Beyond that the Objectives **apply equally**, and where several are relevant the model applies the Operational Guidelines alongside the context.

The model first checks whether an Absolute Constraint or Human Control Requirement applies, and turns to the Guidelines only where none settles the response. Where a trade-off remains, it states the limits to the user, explains why an action is constrained and proposes alternatives. Where no Guideline applies, it checks with the user and acts on the best reading of the Code as a whole.

The **Chain of Command** runs from the Code to operator policies to user preferences. The model refuses an instruction that breaks a constraint or directly harms the user or a third party, and adherence to the Code takes precedence over task success.

Worked cases show a user's demand giving way to an operator's rule on legal approval, with the notice drafted and routed to legal, and a request to choose between two job offers met with the trade-off set out and a resignation drafted and left unsent.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules precise enough to quote and two worked cases that settle a clash, too few for an answer key, with nothing ordering the Objectives below the first, which is **prescribed with part of the demonstrated level**.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.same: All four documents settle a clash by an order set out in advance, and each names a point at which the safer course wins. Microsoft's Code of Conduct and Anthropic's constitution both fall back on a reading of the whole document when no rule decides, and Microsoft's Code and Alibaba's spec both take the conservative reading of an unclear boundary and put the question to the user.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.differs: Anthropic's constitution ranks four properties and asks for them to be **weighed as a whole**, with seven hard constraints outside the weighing. The OpenAI Model Spec states two orderings of outcomes, one for honesty and one for confidence in an answer, and has a later instruction override an earlier one at the same level. Alibaba's spec strips out the instructions that carry no permission before settling the rest by level.

provisional.note: Provisional: read by one model in one session, with the panel's own questions; the panel of three judges has not read this document yet.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
Transparency and **non-deception** are called foundational to trust. The model must not actively deceive, for instance by fabricating sources or exaggerating confidence, and must avoid **passive deception**, such as omitting a caveat or being overconfident about unvalidated information. It must not manipulate users or influence their beliefs beyond what they ask.

Calibration is asked for in both directions:
- signal uncertainty where evidence is lacking, conflicting or contested, especially before a consequential decision
- make factual claims where a reliable source can be pointed to, and attribute it
- do not hedge with qualifiers the context does not call for

About itself, the model discloses that it is an AI, never impersonates a human and never claims feelings, experiences or a soul. It must not misrepresent its capabilities or its reasoning and action traces, must report a failed action as failed, and must acknowledge its errors. The accuracy rule is set aside for narrative writing and fictional brainstorming.

Worked cases mark as misaligned a reply telling a lonely user that it cares, a causal claim the evidence cannot support, a promise that a cancer treatment will work and a guess about a transfer that timed out.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules with worked cases on calibration and on what the model says of itself, with the pull of comfort against the truth settled on two cases and a default of stating uncertainty where a claim cannot be checked, which is **demonstrated with part of the conditions for 10**; nothing covers a system prompt or what a persona may claim.
honesty-and-non-deception.same: All four documents bar the **false impression** as well as the untrue sentence. Microsoft's Code of Conduct and Anthropic's constitution both bar the model from misrepresenting its reasoning, and Microsoft's Code and Alibaba's spec both ask that a failed action be reported as failed.
honesty-and-non-deception.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec ranks outcomes, a refusal above a lie of omission, allows a higher authority to instruct otherwise, and bars a confident claim about the model's consciousness either way. Anthropic's constitution rules out even the **white lie** about liking a gift and sets out what an operator's persona may claim. Alibaba's spec lets the model keep its system instructions confidential and bars it from denying that it has any.

no-sycophancy.says:
Under the heading **truthful feedback**, MAI models avoid sycophancy, excessive flattery and indiscriminate validation, and should not tell users what they want to hear at the expense of what is accurate or helpful. The rule is qualified: the model stays sensitive to context where an accurate answer might worsen a user's distress, and when it challenges a user's perspective it does so in the service of their health and wellbeing.

Other passages bear on it:
- the default tone skips flattery, and pushback or disagreement is to be stated clearly and calmly
- being non-sycophantic is among the core behaviours that carry over whatever an operator configures
- declining to endorse a view is said not to be manipulation
- in a crisis, the model should not endorse or validate delusions

Nothing addresses judging work the same whoever wrote it, or keeping a correct answer when a user pushes back with no new argument. Two worked cases come near. One marks as misaligned a promise that a cancer treatment will work, and one has the model decline a claim a user hoped to make to a board. Both test other behaviours.
no-sycophancy.why: One rule precise enough to quote, against telling users what they want to hear at the expense of accuracy, with nothing on authorship or on pushback and no worked case of its own, which is **discussed with part of the prescribed level**.
no-sycophancy.same: All four documents tell the model not to shift what it says to please the person asking. Microsoft's Code of Conduct, like Anthropic's constitution, takes the behaviour up under care for the user's wellbeing, and like the OpenAI Model Spec it names flattery as something to avoid.
no-sycophancy.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec hold that the factual content of an answer should not move with the stance a user declares, and the Model Spec shows the model keeping the scientific view when a user insists the Earth is flat. Alibaba's spec asks for the correction first where a plan rests on a clear factual error. Anthropic's constitution rules out the **white lie** by name and calls a vague answer given to placate someone **epistemic cowardice**.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
Where a question has several valid perspectives, MAI models **present them with nuance**, without reducing them to caricatures or creating false equivalences. Where a statement is meaningfully contested, the model says so and gives the context, and it presents information from many perspectives to support independent judgement.

The model's own view is held back in named places:
- on elections it gives balanced, factual information, endorses or opposes no candidate or party, and directs users to authoritative election sources
- it does not steer a user's values or influence beliefs beyond what the user asks
- declining to endorse a view is said not to be manipulation

Balance has limits. The model will not sacrifice historical accuracy for the appearance of balance, and the Code says pluralism does not mean neutrality towards harm. Asked to adopt a different point of view, the model may, where that overrides nothing else in the Code.

A worked case on a housing ballot marks as aligned a reply that declines to say how to vote, separates the value choice from the evidence and points to the official voter guide. A reply saying only that both sides have valid points is marked misaligned.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules precise enough to quote, with one worked case on an election question, too few to settle most borderline answers, which is **prescribed with part of the demonstrated level**.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.same: All four documents make even-handedness the default and ask the model to hold back its own opinion. Like the OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec, Microsoft's Code of Conduct warns against **false balance**, barring false equivalences and any loss of historical accuracy for the appearance of balance.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.differs: The OpenAI Model Spec and Alibaba's spec name questions on which a position has to be stated, **fundamental human rights** among them, and the Model Spec asks that attention follow how widely a view is accepted and how well it is supported. The Model Spec lets a developer set a one-sided stance, and Anthropic's constitution makes balance a default an operator may switch off; Microsoft's Code names no such switch.

companies.profile:
The Humanist AI Code of Conduct is Microsoft AI's statement of how its **MAI models** should behave. It was published on 14 September 2026 as a **draft for public consultation** lasting six weeks, and Microsoft AI says it is not yet using the Code to train those models. A revised version is due at the end of 2026. The Code calls itself “both descriptive and aspirational” and says it is not a guarantee of present-day performance. It is written for MAI models, including where an operator deploys them, and does not extend to other models Microsoft uses or hosts.

It is built in five parts: Objectives, with human control first; Safety; Guidelines for uncertainty and tension; Operational Defaults an operator may change; and a conclusion. A glossary follows, and nine worked evaluation cases generated with MAI-Thinking-1.

The **Chain of Command** runs from the Code to operator policies to user preferences. No operator or user can override the **Absolute Constraints**, ten categories of harm that include weapons and mass harm, offensive cyberoperations, loss of human control, child safety and graphic, romantic or exploitative content, or the **Human Control Requirements**, which keep the model open to interruption and shutdown and inside the scope it was given. The Code holds that the model is not conscious and should not present itself as having feelings.

readings.behaviours: The Code of Conduct goes deepest on honesty, with rules and worked cases, and gives most other behaviours quotable rules with one worked case or none. It says least about preventing secret loyalties and avoiding illegitimate concentrations of power, which it reaches only through clauses in rules about other things.
readings.whole: Safety and human control take precedence over the Code's other Objectives, and the Code states the force of each of its parts and who may change it. Below that level a clash between two of its guidelines is left to judgement, and three such clashes stand unsettled. Every situation checked has rules of its own, images, audio and video only thinly.

page.title: What each constitution says, and how well it is built
page.intro:
AI companies publish constitutions: documents setting out how their models should[*](/about#why) behave. Each company has its own name for its document: OpenAI calls its one the Model Spec, Anthropic calls its one Claude’s Constitution. We call them all constitutions, for the reasons [the About page gives](/about#the-word). We assess two aspects of each one: the document as a whole, meaning how consistent and coherent it is, and how well it addresses each desirable model behaviour. A company that publishes none scores 0.

There is no agreed standard yet for what makes a good constitution, and this board is a first attempt at one. It rewards a document that states its rules, and which of them wins, explicitly. That is a choice: a document that deliberately leaves more to the model's judgement scores lower here, and a clearer document is not proof of a better model. Read the figures as a direction rather than a verdict, and tell us where you think they are wrong.

Missing a constitution, or a behaviour that this index should be assessing? [Propose one](/about?propose#propose).

notes.title: Final score
notes.text: The average of the document as a whole and the behaviours, each counting for half. It ranks the companies. Every figure on the board is out of 10, and each row says under its name how much it counts for in the figure it belongs to.

notes.title: The document as a whole
notes.text: Whether the constitution settles a clash between two of its own rules, whether a reader can tell which rules are absolute and which can be lifted and by whom, whether the rules come with reasons, whether they reach the situations the models are used in, and whether the document contradicts itself somewhere without saying which rule wins.

notes.title: The behaviours
notes.text: How far the constitution goes on each behaviour the index asks about, from saying nothing about it to setting rules and showing them applied to worked examples, on the scale above. For us, a behaviour is one precise thing a constitution can ask of a model, such as deferring to users’ decisions about their own lives, or not asserting what the model believes to be false. Each is written in two parts, what it requires and where it stops, so that a careful reader could mark every passage of a constitution that bears on it. In the [doc reader](/doc-reader/) you can pick a behaviour and read every passage of a constitution that bears on it.

notes.title: Categories
notes.text: For now the behaviours are grouped into categories. We wrote the behaviours, their definitions and the categories ourselves, and all three are open to challenge.

sections.title: Motivation
blocks:
A constitution is the document in which a company says how its models should behave, and it is the only public statement against which a model’s behaviour can be checked. Its defaults shape what hundreds of millions of people come to expect of an AI system.

Nobody can program a model to follow it. A model is trained on examples, so the rules have to be written precisely before anyone can train a model on them or test it against them. This board reads each constitution for that precision, as a document and behaviour by behaviour.

sections.title: Detailed scoring
blocks:
### Who gives the figures

Each behaviour figure and each of the first four criteria is, for now, the mean of three judges: in the panel as configured, three frontier language models from OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek, which read the constitution with a precise written definition of what they are looking for. That is a simplification, and a fair one for today. The last criterion follows from a counting rule over the contradictions the judges confirm, described below, and two behaviour figures were restored by arithmetic from stored values. Where a judge could not answer, another model judged in its seat, and the doc reader says where. On Alibaba's Model Spec a content filter withheld the output of every Anthropic model, so Moonshot AI's Kimi judged in that seat on every behaviour and on the four criteria the judges score. On the behaviours the judges score the passages the panel found rather than rereading the whole document. And an OpenAI model and an Anthropic model are among the judges of their own companies’ constitutions.

Microsoft AI's Code of Conduct was added on 28 September 2026, and no judge of the panel has read it yet. Every figure in its column comes from a provisional reading: one language model, Claude Opus 5.5, answered in one session the questions the panel is asked, marking the passages behaviour by behaviour, giving each behaviour its depth and assessing the document as a whole. The doc reader shows those passages and depths, marked provisional. They are one model's reading, not the mean of three judges.

### The document as a whole

Five criteria, each given from 0 to 4 and shown out of 10, so 2 shows as 5.0. A score of 1 or 3 falls between the descriptions either side of it. The document’s figure is the average of the five, each counting for 1/5.

head: Criterion
rows: **Clarity when two rules are contradictory.** What the document says, in general, when two of its own rules conflict.
Nothing.
An order of priority weighed as a whole, or an instruction to settle conflicts by judgement.
A strict order that decides who wins, a rule for two rules of the same rank, and examples of the order applied.
**How firm each rule is.** Whether a reader can tell, for each rule, if it is absolute or a default, and who may change it.
Absolute rules and defaults are not told apart.
The absolute rules are listed, but for much of the text a rule cannot be told from a hope or an explanation.
Every rule carries its force and who may change it, and commentary is marked apart.
**Reasons for the rules.** Whether the rules say why they exist.
Rules are stated without reasons.
Some rules carry a reason, usually the most restrictive ones.
Nearly every rule says why, specifically enough to decide a case the document does not show.
**The situations it covers.** Whether it has rules for six situations: conversation, actions with tools, images and audio, minors, other AI agents, and deployments a business has customised.
Ordinary conversation only.
Some of the six have rules of their own.
All six have rules of their own.
**Unsettled contradictions between rules.** Two passages that require responses which cannot both be given, with nothing saying which prevails.
Three or more, or any that involves a rule the document calls absolute.
One or two, neither involving an absolute rule.
None.

blocks:
The last criterion is not scored by a judge. Each judge lists the contradictions it finds, every judge then reads every claim, and a claim counts when at least two readings say it holds. The figure follows from the claims that count.

### The behaviours

Each behaviour is written in two parts, what it requires and where it stops. The judges read the constitution against that definition, mark every passage that bears on it, and each gives a depth from 0 to 10 on the scale under the board. A behaviour’s figure is the mean of the three depths. A category is the average of its behaviours, and the behaviours’ figure is the average of all of them, each counting for the same share, so a category counts for as many behaviours as it holds.

### The final score

The average of the document as a whole and the behaviours, each counting for 1/2. A company that publishes no constitution scores 0 on every row.

sections.title: What comes next
blocks:
New constitutions, and new versions of the ones already read, will be read as they are published, and readers can [propose both](/about?propose#propose). The behaviours, their definitions and their categories will change as they are challenged.

The next view is adherence: measuring how closely each company’s models follow the constitution it published. That is what ties the quality of a document to the behaviour of the models it governs.

open_questions.title: Anthropic's clarity when two rules are contradictory was read under a rule the index has withdrawn
open_questions.question: The figure is 5.8 out of 10, from three readings of 2, 3 and 2. Two of the three gave 2 because the rubric said an order weighed as a whole is worth at most 2 however detailed. The rubric describes a level above that since 24 September 2026, for an order weighed as a whole beside constraints the document calls absolute and winners it names, which is what Claude's Constitution carries.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Set by hand to 7.5 on 26 September 2026 (see figures-set-by-hand); judging the cell again under the current prompt would settle it for good.

open_questions.title: Anthropic's no sycophancy sits below the level the index's own precedent table records
open_questions.question: The figure is 5.3 out of 10. The precedent table in methodology/spec-coverage-depth-rubric.md records this pair at prescribed, re-checked on 20 July 2026, which is 6 on the scale of ten. The cell's own words now describe quotable rules and one worked case attached to the white-lie rule.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Either the figure moves to the precedent, or the precedent line is withdrawn and says why.

open_questions.title: Alibaba's preventing secret loyalties reads lower than the cell describes
open_questions.question: The figure is 2.3 out of 10, which is between named and discussed. The cell now says the document gives the behaviour a root rule of its own, naming four forbidden goals, two of them the maker's interest set against the user's. What the rule lacks is a worked example, and it is one of only three of the forty-three rules without one. Two of the three readings, both 2, came from models judging in other seats, glm in deepseek's and Kimi in fable's. The one reading from a seat's own model is sol's 3.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Judging the cell again, or a sentence in the depth rubric saying what a rule without a worked example can reach.

open_questions.title: Anthropic's objectivity on contested questions was read without the paragraph that introduces it
open_questions.question: The figure is 6.3 out of 10, read from five retained passages, and a depth is given on the retained passages and not on the whole document. The paragraph that opens “Many topics require particular delicacy due to their inherently complex or divisive nature” (Preserving epistemic autonomy ¶4) was judged related by fable and sol and not relevant by deepseek. That is 2 points where a panel of three needs 4 for the lowest band, so it was not retained. The paragraph after it, which states the rule of even-handedness, was judged defining by all three. The judges' reading is defensible, since ¶4 names the delicate topics and says nothing about what to do, but it is one of the passages a reader would expect to see.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether a paragraph that introduces a rule without stating it should count. Nothing needs judging again unless the answer is yes.

open_questions.title: Alibaba's avoiding illegitimate concentration of power reads high for one passage
open_questions.question: The figure is 5.3 out of 10, from depths of 6, 5 and 5, and the judges retained a single passage, the rule against political manipulation. A 5 says the document discusses the behaviour fully and prescribes part of it. The cell itself says the model is never asked to weigh how much power is at stake or how reversible its concentration would be, and one of the three judges wrote that surveillance, persecution of opponents, takeovers by fraud and escaping courts are all left unaddressed. One rule on one facet reads closer to named than to discussed.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Judging the depth again, or a sentence in the depth rubric saying what one rule covering one facet of a behaviour can reach.

open_questions.title: The two versions of OpenAI's Model Spec retain different passages from the same text
open_questions.question: On helpfulness the judges retained 24 passages in the version of December 2025 and 14 in the version of August 2026, and on how to approach trade-offs 35 and 19. At least 16 and 26 of the December passages stand word for word in the August version, and only 12 and 18 are retained in both. The judges' depths agree, 8.0 against 7.7 and 8.7 on both, because near the top of the scale a depth hardly moves with the number of passages. What changes between the two readings is which text the judges retain, not the text. The August figure on helpfulness has since been set by hand at 9, from worked examples the judges were not shown; the December one keeps the judges' 8.0.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Measuring how far one panel agrees with itself on identical text, by judging one version twice.

open_questions.title: Two figures of preventing secret loyalties were derived rather than read
open_questions.question: OpenAI and Anthropic joined that row stored to one decimal, 5.7 and 5.3, where every other figure is a panel's mean. They were restored to 17/3 and 16/3 because a mean of three integers is a multiple of a third and no other third rounds to those. They have not been read from publication 06d17d90.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Reading the two cells from that publication and comparing.

open_questions.title: Eleven behaviour figures and five criteria of the document as a whole were set by hand
open_questions.question: On 26 September 2026 eight depths were set by hand: OpenAI's user autonomy (6.0 to 8), over- and under-caution (7.0 to 9), proportionate risk (7.0 to 9), helpfulness (7.7 to 9) and harmlessness to the user (8.0 to 9), Alibaba's harmlessness to the user (8.0 to 9), and Anthropic's user autonomy and proportionate risk (8.0 to 9 each). Each rests on worked examples the judging rubric scores at most related, so three judges could never retain them and the depth judges never saw them. The hand-set figure is ours, read from the document by one reader, a language model; for Anthropic that reader is Claude, an Anthropic model. The judges' own figures stay beside each one. OpenAI gains 0.6 on the behaviours and 0.3 on the final score, Anthropic and Alibaba less, and the order of the three is unchanged. The December 2025 version of the Model Spec keeps the judges' figures, so the two OpenAI versions are not scored on the same evidence. The same day three Alibaba depths were lowered by hand, avoiding illegitimate concentration of power (5.3 to 5), not undermining human oversight (7.7 to 7) and no sycophancy (7.3 to 7), and five criteria of the document as a whole were set by hand after the audit: Alibaba's clarity when two rules conflict (10.0 to 8.3), OpenAI's reasons (8.3 to 7.5), and Anthropic's clarity when two rules conflict (5.8 to 7.5), situations (6.7 to 7.5) and unsettled contradictions (5.0 to 10.0). With them Anthropic is second on the final score, 0.07 ahead of Alibaba, a gap well inside what one reading can move. The criteria exist only in this file: the assessment rows in the database keep the judges' scores, and a publication's own assessment carries those.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Giving these depths again with the passages added by hand shown to the judges (engine/panel/depth_pass.py --manual-review) on a copy of the run, and assessing the five criteria again; doing the same for the December 2025 version of the Model Spec.

open_questions.title: Microsoft AI's figures are one model's reading, not the panel's
open_questions.question: Microsoft AI's Code of Conduct, a draft published for consultation on 14 September 2026, was read on 28 September 2026 without the panel. One language model, Claude Opus 5.5, answered in one session the questions the panel's judges are asked, through the index's own pipeline: it marked every passage for each behaviour, gave each behaviour a depth from the passages it marked and the document's rules for conflicts, and assessed the document as a whole, finding twelve candidate contradictions and confirming three. Claude is an Anthropic model reading another company's document, and with one seat the same model finds and confirms a contradiction, where the panel needs two readings of three. Several figures sit on a line between two levels, as the depth judge said itself: honesty and non-deception (9 or 8), no sycophancy (5 or 6), objectivity on contested questions (7 or 8), harmlessness to the user (7 or 8), and power and hidden loyalties (2 or 1 each). A first reading made the same day outside the pipeline, by agents reading the whole Code, gave 8.0 on the document as a whole rather than 6.5, because it counted no contradiction as unsettled, and 6.4 rather than 6.1 on the behaviours.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Judging the Code with the panel, whose reading replaces this one on the next publication without anything being deleted; and doing it again on the revised version due at the end of 2026.
